entries.1:1: God spoke to Moses from the tent where the people met with him. This shows that what follows comes directly from God, not from Moses' own ideas.
entries.1:2: God told Moses to give the Israelites rules for giving offerings to him, and those offerings were to come from their own animals. It means giving to God was to come from what people already had.
entries.1:3: If someone gave a bull as a whole burnt offering, it had to be a healthy male with nothing wrong with it, brought to the tent entrance. The point was to give God your best, not a flawed leftover.
entries.1:4: The person placed his hands on the animal's head, and the offering was accepted on his behalf to deal with his sin. It showed that guilt was being transferred and forgiveness was being asked for.
entries.1:5: The animal was killed in front of the Lord, and the priests splashed its blood on and around the altar at the tent entrance. Blood was central because it stood for life given up on the person's behalf.
entries.1:6: The animal was skinned and cut into pieces. This was careful, orderly preparation, showing that the offering was handled with seriousness.
entries.1:7: The priests were to build the fire on the altar and arrange the wood. The priests had a specific job to do in making the offering happen.
entries.1:8: The priests laid the pieces, the head, and the fat in order on the burning wood. Everything was arranged deliberately, not thrown together.
entries.1:9: The inner organs and legs were washed with water, and then the whole animal was burned on the altar as a pleasing smell to the Lord. Clean preparation mattered, and the whole offering was given over to God.
entries.1:10: If the offering was a sheep or goat, it also had to be a healthy male with nothing wrong with it. The same standard of giving God your best applied to smaller animals too.
entries.1:11: The animal was killed on the north side of the altar, and the priests put some of its blood on and around the altar. The location and the blood were both part of how the offering was made properly.
entries.1:12: The animal was cut into pieces, and the priest arranged the parts, head, and fat on the burning wood. The offering was laid out carefully before being burned.
entries.1:13: The inner organs and legs were washed, and then the priest burned the whole animal on the altar as a pleasing smell to the Lord. Cleanliness and completeness were both required.
entries.1:14: If someone's burnt offering was a bird, they were to bring doves or young pigeons. This made it possible for poorer people to give an offering too.
entries.1:15: The priest brought the bird to the altar, killed it, burned it, and drained its blood against the side of the altar. Even the smallest offering was handled with the same care and blood ritual.
entries.1:16: The priest removed the bird's stomach and feathers and put them beside the altar where the ashes were dumped. The parts not burned were disposed of in the proper place.
entries.1:17: The bird was opened at the wings but not torn in two, then burned on the altar as a pleasing smell to the Lord. The offering was still whole in a sense, and it was fully given to God.
entries.2:1: This describes a gift of fine flour mixed with oil and incense, brought to God as a grain offering. It means God deserves our best, not our leftovers.
entries.2:2: The priest burns a handful of the flour, oil, and incense as a reminder that the whole gift belongs to God. It shows that even a small, faithful act of worship is pleasing to him.
entries.2:3: The leftover grain belongs to the priests as their food, and it is treated as very holy. It means those who serve God are to be cared for from what is given to him.
entries.2:4: If the grain gift is baked in an oven, it must be made without yeast and mixed with oil. It teaches that worship should be done the way God asks, not however we prefer.
entries.2:5: A grain gift cooked on a griddle must also be made of the best flour, without yeast, and mixed with oil. It means God's instructions apply to every form our giving takes.
entries.2:6: The cooked grain is broken into pieces and oil is poured on it before it is offered. It shows that careful preparation is part of honoring God.
entries.2:7: A grain gift cooked in a pan must be made of the best flour mixed with oil. It means the same standard of quality applies no matter how the gift is prepared.
entries.2:8: The person brings the prepared grain gift to the Lord, and the priest carries it to the altar. It means our gifts reach God through the priest who represents him.
entries.2:9: The priest burns a portion as a reminder, and it is described as a pleasing smell to the Lord. It means God accepts the offering given with the right heart.
entries.2:10: The rest of the grain gift goes to the priests and is considered very holy. It means God provides for his servants through the offerings brought to him.
entries.2:11: No grain gift offered to God may contain yeast, and yeast or honey must never be burned on the altar. It teaches that some things, though ordinary, are not fitting in worship offered to God.
entries.2:12: Yeast and honey may be brought as first-fruit gifts, but they must not be burned on the altar. It means not everything acceptable as a gift is acceptable as an offering by fire.
entries.2:13: Every grain gift must be seasoned with salt, which stands for God's lasting agreement with his people. It means our worship should reflect his faithfulness and be pure and lasting.
entries.2:14: A first-fruit grain gift is made from new grain that has been dried or roasted over fire and crushed. It means the first and best of what God gives us should be offered back to him.
entries.2:15: Oil and incense are added to this first-fruit grain gift. It means even the simplest offering is to be given with care and devotion.
entries.2:16: The priest burns part of the grain, part of the oil, and all the incense as a reminder offering to the Lord. It means God is honored when his portion is given fully and faithfully.
entries.3:1: This describes a peace offering from a herd animal, which had to be healthy and without defects. For the reader, it shows that gifts brought to God were to be the best, not leftovers.
entries.3:2: The person placed a hand on the animal's head and killed it at the entrance of the meeting tent, and the priests applied its blood to the altar. This showed the offerer identifying with the sacrifice and that life belongs to God.
entries.3:3: Part of the peace offering was burned on the altar as a gift to God, specifically the fat around the inner organs. It teaches that the offering was shared with God in a special way.
entries.3:4: The kidneys and the fat around them and near the liver were removed for burning. These were considered the richest parts, reserved for God.
entries.3:5: The priests burned these parts on the altar on top of the regular burnt offering, and the smell was pleasing to God. It shows worship was offered in the way God asked, not however people preferred.
entries.3:6: A peace offering could also come from the flock, again male or female but with no defect. The point is that God accepted either sex but required the animal to be sound.
entries.3:7: If the offering was a lamb, it was first presented before the Lord. This act of bringing it into God's presence marked it as set apart for him.
entries.3:8: The offerer laid a hand on the lamb's head and killed it before the meeting tent, and the priests put its blood around the altar. The blood was handled carefully because it represented life.
entries.3:9: From the peace offering, the fat tail and the fat around the inner organs were given to God as a burned offering. The best portions were set aside for him.
entries.3:10: The kidneys and their surrounding fat, along with the fat near the liver, were removed. These specific parts were reserved for burning on the altar.
entries.3:11: The priest burned this on the altar as food for the offering made by fire to the Lord. The language pictures the altar as God's table receiving the offering.
entries.3:12: If the peace offering was a goat, it too was brought before the Lord. Every kind of acceptable offering had to be presented to God first.
entries.3:13: The offerer laid a hand on the goat's head and killed it before the meeting tent, and the priests applied its blood around the altar. The same careful procedure applied to every animal.
entries.3:14: The offerer brought the fat covering and around the inner organs as a gift burned to the Lord. The richest inner parts were given to God.
entries.3:15: The kidneys with their fat and the fat near the liver were removed for the offering. These parts were consistently set apart for God.
entries.3:16: The priest burned them on the altar as food for the fire offering, a pleasing smell, and all the fat belonged to the Lord. This teaches that God claims the richest portions for himself.
entries.3:17: This was a permanent rule for all generations and homes: the people must not eat fat or blood. For the reader, it shows that God sets boundaries and that blood, which stands for life, is treated as sacred.
entries.4:1: God is speaking directly to Moses, giving him instructions to pass on. This shows that what follows comes from God himself, not from Moses' own ideas.
entries.4:2: This rule is for people who sin by accident or mistake, not on purpose, breaking one of God's commands. It means God made a way for honest mistakes to be dealt with, not just deliberate rebellion.
entries.4:3: If the high priest sins, his failure affects the whole nation, so he must bring a perfect young bull as an offering. It shows that leaders carry extra responsibility because their wrong choices can lead others astray.
entries.4:4: The priest brings the animal to the entrance of the meeting tent, lays his hands on it, and kills it there. Laying hands on the animal symbolically puts the guilt onto it, showing that sin costs a life.
entries.4:5: The high priest carries some of the animal's blood into the meeting tent. Blood represented life, and it was central to making things right with God.
entries.4:6: He dips his finger in the blood and sprinkles it seven times in front of the curtain of the holy place. Seven signals completeness, and the sprinkling shows the cleansing reaching into God's holy presence.
entries.4:7: Some blood goes on the corners of the incense altar inside the tent, and the rest is poured out at the base of the outdoor altar. This shows that the sin affected both the holy place and the everyday place of worship.
entries.4:8: The priest removes all the fat from the animal's inner parts. The fat was considered the richest, best part, set aside for God.
entries.4:9: He also takes the kidneys and the fat around them and near the liver. These specific inner parts were given to God as part of the offering.
entries.4:10: The fat is handled the same way as in the peace offering and burned on the altar. This connects the sin offering to the regular pattern of worship God had already set.
entries.4:11: The skin, flesh, head, legs, inner parts, and waste of the bull are left over. These parts were not burned on the altar.
entries.4:12: The whole remaining animal is carried outside the camp to a clean place and burned there. Sin was taken outside the community, showing it had to be removed, not just covered over.
entries.4:13: This covers the case where the whole nation sins unknowingly and becomes guilty without realizing it. Guilt before God can exist even when people are unaware of what they did.
entries.4:14: Once the sin becomes known, the community must bring a young bull as a sin offering to the meeting tent. When people learn of their wrong, they are expected to respond, not ignore it.
entries.4:15: The elders of the community lay their hands on the bull's head and kill it before the Lord. The leaders act on behalf of all the people, identifying the whole nation with the offering.
entries.4:16: The priest carries some of the bull's blood into the meeting tent. As with the high priest's offering, the blood is brought near to God's presence.
entries.4:17: He sprinkles the blood seven times with his finger in front of the curtain. The same careful ritual is repeated, showing the seriousness of the nation's sin.
entries.4:18: Some blood goes on the horns of the incense altar, and the rest is poured at the base of the outdoor altar. The blood is applied in the places where God meets his people.
entries.4:19: All the fat is removed and burned on the altar. The best parts are given to God as part of the offering.
entries.4:20: The priest does with this bull exactly what he did with the earlier sin offering, and the result is that the people are forgiven. God's forgiveness comes through the offering he himself prescribed.
entries.4:21: The rest of the bull is taken outside the camp and burned, just like the first one, because it is the sin offering for the whole people. The sin is carried away from the community.
entries.4:22: This case is for a leader who sins by mistake and becomes guilty. Leaders are held to the same standard of obedience to God's commands.
entries.4:23: Once the leader realizes his sin, he must bring a perfect male goat as his offering. Awareness of sin is meant to lead to action, not just regret.
entries.4:24: He lays his hand on the goat's head and kills it where the burnt offering is killed. The offering is made in the proper place and in the proper way God required.
entries.4:25: The priest puts some of the blood on the corners of the outdoor altar and pours the rest at its base. The blood is applied to the altar where daily worship happened.
entries.4:26: The fat is burned on the altar like the peace offering, and the priest makes atonement so the leader is forgiven. Forgiveness is the stated outcome of following God's instructions.
entries.4:27: This covers an ordinary person who sins by mistake and becomes guilty. No one is too unimportant for God to address; everyday people are included in these rules.
entries.4:28: When the person becomes aware of the sin, they bring a perfect female goat. The offering is smaller than a leader's, but the requirement to deal with sin is the same.
entries.4:29: The person lays a hand on the goat's head and kills it where the burnt offering is killed. The sinner personally identifies with the offering.
entries.4:30: The priest puts some blood on the altar's corners and pours the rest at its base. The blood is handled carefully, just as in the other cases.
entries.4:31: The fat is removed like in the peace offering and burned as a pleasing smell to the Lord, and the person is forgiven. Even a small offering, done God's way, brings real forgiveness.
entries.4:32: If the person brings a lamb instead, it must be a perfect female. God allowed some flexibility in what animal was brought, but it still had to be without defect.
entries.4:33: The person lays a hand on the lamb's head and kills it as a sin offering where the burnt offering is killed. The same pattern of identification and sacrifice applies.
entries.4:34: The priest puts some blood on the altar's corners and pours the rest at its base. The blood ritual is consistent with the other sin offerings.
entries.4:35: The fat is removed like in the peace offering and burned on the altar as an offering to the Lord, and the person is forgiven. The chapter ends by repeating the promise: following God's way brings forgiveness.
entries.5:1: If you know the truth about something and are asked under oath to speak, staying silent is itself wrong. The reader learns that failing to speak up when called to testify makes you accountable for the truth.
entries.5:2: Touching something unclean, even by accident without realizing it, still leaves a person ritually unclean. The reader sees that carelessness in daily life can make a person guilty before God, even when it was not intended.
entries.5:3: The same applies to accidentally touching something unclean connected with a person; once you realize it, you are guilty. The reader learns that guilt begins when you become aware of what happened, and then you must deal with it.
entries.5:4: If someone rashly swears an oath to do something good or bad without thinking it through, they are guilty once they realize it. The reader is warned that careless words spoken as promises matter and carry responsibility.
entries.5:5: Anyone who becomes guilty in these ways must openly admit the wrong they have done. The reader learns that confession, saying the wrong out loud, is the first step toward making things right.
entries.5:6: The guilty person brings a female lamb or goat as a sin offering, and the priest makes atonement for them. The reader sees that wrongdoing requires a real cost and that God provided a way for forgiveness.
entries.5:7: If someone is too poor for a lamb, they may bring two doves or two young pigeons instead, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering. The reader learns that God's requirement for forgiveness does not depend on wealth.
entries.5:8: The priest offers the sin offering first, wringing its neck without severing it completely. The reader sees that the ritual was carried out in a specific, careful way as God commanded.
entries.5:9: The priest sprinkles some of the blood on the side of the altar and pours the rest at its base. The reader learns that blood was central to the offering that dealt with sin.
entries.5:10: The second bird is offered as a burnt offering according to the law, and the priest makes atonement so the person is forgiven. The reader sees that forgiveness comes through the offering God prescribed, not through the person's own effort.
entries.5:11: If someone cannot afford even two birds, they may bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, with no oil or incense because it is a sin offering. The reader learns that even the poorest person had a way to bring their sin before God.
entries.5:12: The person brings the flour to the priest, who takes a handful and burns it on the altar as a memorial portion to the Lord. The reader sees that the offering was presented to God in a set way, even when it was only flour.
entries.5:13: The priest makes atonement and the person is forgiven, and the rest of the flour belongs to the priest like a grain offering. The reader learns that forgiveness was fully available even to those with the least to give.
entries.5:14: This verse simply introduces that the Lord spoke these next instructions to Moses. The reader sees that what follows is presented as God's own command given through his leader.
entries.5:15: If someone unintentionally sins regarding the holy things of the Lord, they must bring a flawless male sheep valued in silver by the sanctuary standard. The reader learns that even accidental offenses against what belongs to God require serious restitution.
entries.5:16: The person must pay back what was wronged plus a fifth of its value, and the priest makes atonement with the ram so they are forgiven. The reader sees that making things right includes paying back more than was taken.
entries.5:17: If someone breaks one of the Lord's commands without knowing it, they are still guilty and responsible. The reader learns that ignorance does not erase guilt before God.
entries.5:18: They bring a flawless male sheep of the set value as a guilt offering, and the priest makes atonement for the unintentional sin so they are forgiven. The reader sees that God provided a way to deal with even unknown wrongdoing.
entries.5:19: This is a guilt offering because the person is truly guilty before the Lord. The reader learns that guilt before God is real and must be acknowledged and dealt with, not ignored.
entries.6:1: God is speaking to Moses, giving him instructions to pass on to the people. This verse simply sets up the rules that follow.
entries.6:2: If someone cheats a neighbor—by lying about property left in their care, by not repaying a debt, by stealing, or by mistreating them—God treats that as unfaithfulness to him too. It means wronging people is also an offense against God, not just a private matter.
entries.6:3: This adds lying under oath about something found and denied. If a person does any of these wrongs, they are guilty and must answer for it.
entries.6:4: Once they realize their guilt, they must return what they took or kept dishonestly—whether by force, by cruelty, or by holding back something entrusted to them. Real repentance starts with giving back what was wrongfully taken.
entries.6:5: They must repay the full amount plus one-fifth extra to the rightful owner, once they are found guilty. The extra makes up for the loss and shows genuine sorrow for the wrong.
entries.6:6: Then they bring a ram without defect to the priest as a guilt offering, valued at the set rate. Making things right with the person comes first, then the offering to God.
entries.6:7: The priest makes atonement for them before the Lord, and they are forgiven for whatever wrong they did. God offers real forgiveness once the wrong is made right.
entries.6:8: God continues speaking to Moses, introducing the next set of instructions. This verse just marks a new section of the law.
entries.6:9: God gives Aaron and his sons the rules for the burnt offering: it stays on the altar fire all night until morning, and the fire must never go out. The fire's constant burning showed the people's ongoing devotion to God.
entries.6:10: The priest puts on his linen clothes and underwear and removes the ashes from the altar, placing them beside it. Even handling leftovers from worship was done carefully and respectfully.
entries.6:11: He then changes out of his holy clothes, puts on ordinary ones, and carries the ashes to a clean place outside the camp. The sacred and the everyday were kept distinct.
entries.6:12: The altar fire must never go out; each morning the priest adds wood, arranges the burnt offering, and burns the fat of the peace offerings. Faithful daily attention kept worship going.
entries.6:13: The fire on the altar must burn continually and never be allowed to go out. This constant flame pictured unbroken devotion and God's ongoing presence with his people.
entries.6:14: This gives the rules for the grain offering, which Aaron's sons present to the Lord in front of the altar. It was a gift of thanks and honor brought to God.
entries.6:15: The priest takes a handful of the flour, oil, and all the incense and burns it on the altar as a memorial, a pleasing smell to the Lord. A portion was offered to God to represent the whole gift.
entries.6:16: The rest of the grain offering belongs to Aaron and his sons, who eat it without yeast in a holy place within the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. God provided for the priests through the offerings brought to him.
entries.6:17: It must not be baked with yeast; it is the priests' share of the fire offerings and is most holy, like the sin and guilt offerings. Yeast often stood for corruption, so it was kept out of these holy gifts.
entries.6:18: Every male descendant of Aaron may eat it as a permanent right through all generations, and anyone who touches these offerings becomes holy. Being near holy things required being set apart for God.
entries.6:19: God speaks again to Moses, beginning a new instruction. This verse simply introduces what follows.
entries.6:20: On the day a priest is ordained, he brings a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a grain offering, half in the morning and half in the evening. The priest's own dedication to God was marked by regular daily offering.
entries.6:21: It is prepared with oil on a griddle, cooked, and broken into pieces and presented as a pleasing smell to the Lord. Careful preparation showed honor toward God.
entries.6:22: The son who succeeds him as priest must offer the same thing forever, and it must be completely burned. This kept the priesthood's dedication continuing from generation to generation.
entries.6:23: Every grain offering brought by a priest for himself must be entirely burned, with none kept for food. Unlike other grain offerings, the priest received no share of his own offering.
entries.6:24: God continues speaking to Moses, introducing the next set of rules. This verse just marks the start of a new section.
entries.6:25: God gives Aaron and his sons the rules for the sin offering: it is killed before the Lord in the same place as the burnt offering and is most holy. Sin had to be dealt with seriously and in the way God prescribed.
entries.6:26: The priest who offers the sin offering eats it in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Part of the offering provided for the priest who ministered.
entries.6:27: Anyone who touches its meat becomes holy, and if any blood splashes on clothing, that clothing must be washed in a holy place. Contact with holy things required cleansing and care.
entries.6:28: A clay pot used to cook the meat must be broken, but a bronze pot must be scrubbed and rinsed with water. Porous clay absorbed the holy meat, so it could not be reused for ordinary purposes.
entries.6:29: Every male among the priests may eat it, because it is most holy. The offering was reserved for those set apart to serve at the altar.
entries.6:30: But if any of the sin offering's blood was brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the holy place, none of that meat may be eaten—it must be burned with fire. Offerings that dealt with sin at the deepest level were not shared but completely given to God.
entries.7:1: This starts the rules for the guilt offering, a sacrifice for when someone has done wrong. It tells the reader that this offering is treated as especially holy, set apart for God.
entries.7:2: The animal for the guilt offering is killed where the whole burnt offering is killed, and the priest puts its blood on and around the altar. Blood is handled carefully because it is central to making things right with God.
entries.7:3: All the fat of the animal, including the fat tail and the fat around the inner organs, is offered to God. The best parts are given to him rather than kept.
entries.7:4: The priest removes the two kidneys with their fat and the fat attached to the liver. These specific parts belong to the offering.
entries.7:5: The priest burns these parts on the altar as a fire offering to the Lord. This is what makes it a guilt offering.
entries.7:6: Only the male priests may eat this offering, and they must eat it in a holy place. It is treated as most holy, so it is handled with care.
entries.7:7: The guilt offering and the sin offering follow the same rule. The priest who performs the ceremony to deal with sin gets to keep the meat.
entries.7:8: When a priest offers someone's burnt offering, he may keep the animal's hide for himself. This is part of how the priests were provided for.
entries.7:9: Grain offerings cooked in an oven, a pot, or on a griddle belong to the priest who offers them. He receives the food he has prepared for God.
entries.7:10: Any grain offering, whether mixed with oil or dry, is shared equally among all the priests. No priest gets more than another from these offerings.
entries.7:11: This begins the rules for peace offerings, which are brought to the Lord. These are offerings shared between God, the priest, and the person bringing them.
entries.7:12: If the offering is given to express thanks, the person brings unleavened cakes mixed with oil and thin cakes spread with oil, made from the finest flour. These accompany the thank offering.
entries.7:13: Along with the thank offering, the person also brings cakes made with yeast. This is part of the peace offering given in thanks.
entries.7:14: One portion from each kind of offering is presented to the Lord and given to the priest who puts the blood on the altar. This is the priest's share.
entries.7:15: The meat of a thank offering must be eaten on the same day it is offered, with nothing left until morning. Thanksgiving is treated as something to be enjoyed promptly.
entries.7:16: If the offering is brought to fulfill a vow or given freely, the meat can be eaten that day and the rest the next day. These offerings allow a little more time than the thank offering.
entries.7:17: Any meat still left on the third day must be burned. It is not to be eaten after that point.
entries.7:18: If someone eats the peace offering meat on the third day, the offering is not accepted and does not count for the person who brought it. The meat becomes unclean, and the person who eats it bears guilt.
entries.7:19: Meat that touches anything unclean must not be eaten but burned. Clean people may eat the meat of the peace offerings.
entries.7:20: Anyone who is unclean but eats the Lord's peace offering meat is cut off from the community. Being unclean and sharing in holy food do not mix.
entries.7:21: Touching something unclean, whether from a person, an animal, or a detestable thing, and then eating the peace offering meat means being cut off from the people. Holiness is taken seriously.
entries.7:22: The Lord speaks to Moses. This introduces the next set of instructions.
entries.7:23: The Israelites are told not to eat the fat of oxen, sheep, or goats. The fat belongs to God and is reserved for the altar.
entries.7:24: Fat from animals that died naturally or were killed by wild beasts can be used for other purposes but must not be eaten. Even in those cases, the fat is not food.
entries.7:25: Anyone who eats the fat of an animal that is used as a fire offering to the Lord is cut off from the people. This rule carries serious consequences.
entries.7:26: The Israelites must not eat any blood, whether from birds or animals, anywhere they live. Blood is not to be consumed.
entries.7:27: Anyone who eats blood is cut off from the people. This is a firm rule with a serious penalty.
entries.7:28: The Lord speaks to Moses again. This begins another set of instructions.
entries.7:29: The person bringing a peace offering to the Lord must present part of it as an offering to him. The worshiper personally brings a portion to God.
entries.7:30: The worshiper brings the fat and the breast of the animal, and the breast is waved before the Lord as a special presentation. This act sets the portion apart for God.
entries.7:31: The priest burns the fat on the altar, but the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons. God receives the fat, and the priests receive the meat.
entries.7:32: The right leg of the peace offering is given to the priest as a contribution. This is another share set aside for those who serve at the altar.
entries.7:33: The priest who offers the blood and the fat of the peace offering gets the right leg as his portion. The one who does the work receives this share.
entries.7:34: God has taken the waved breast and the lifted-up right leg from Israel's peace offerings and given them permanently to Aaron and his sons. This is the priests' lasting share.
entries.7:35: This is the holy portion given to Aaron and his sons from the Lord's fire offerings on the day they were ordained as priests. Their support comes from what is offered to God.
entries.7:36: The Lord commanded Israel to give this to the priests on the day he appointed them, and it is their permanent right for all generations. This provision is meant to last.
entries.7:37: This summarizes the laws for the burnt offering, grain offering, guilt offering, ordination of priests, and peace offerings. It shows these instructions form one connected system of worship.
entries.7:38: The Lord gave these commands to Moses on Mount Sinai when he told Israel to bring their offerings to him in the Sinai wilderness. These rules come directly from God.
entries.8:1: God speaks directly to Moses, giving him the next set of instructions. It reminds the reader that what follows comes from God, not from human invention.
entries.8:2: God tells Moses to bring Aaron and his sons, along with the special clothes, oil, and animals needed for the ceremony. These are the supplies for setting the priests apart for their work.
entries.8:3: The whole community is called to gather at the entrance of the meeting tent to witness this. It shows that the setting apart of priests was a public event, not a private one.
entries.8:4: Moses obeys exactly, and the people assemble as commanded. It shows that obedience to God's instructions was the first step of the whole ceremony.
entries.8:5: Moses tells the people that what they are about to see is commanded by God. It helps the reader understand this ritual was not Moses' idea but God's.
entries.8:6: Moses brings Aaron and his sons forward and washes them with water. This washing shows they must be clean before they can serve God.
entries.8:7: Moses dresses Aaron in the special priestly garments, layer by layer. The careful dressing marks Aaron as set apart for a holy role.
entries.8:8: Moses adds the priestly pouch containing the Urim and Thummim, objects used to seek God's guidance. It shows that the priest's work included helping people know God's will.
entries.8:9: Moses places the turban and gold plate on Aaron's head, exactly as God commanded. The gold crown marks Aaron as dedicated to God's service.
entries.8:10: Moses pours the holy oil on the tent and everything in it to set them apart for God. This shows that the place of worship itself had to be made holy.
entries.8:11: Moses sprinkles oil on the altar, its tools, and the washing basin seven times. The number seven suggests completeness, showing everything was fully set apart for God.
entries.8:12: Moses pours some of the oil on Aaron's head to set him apart. This anointing marks Aaron as chosen and dedicated to serve as priest.
entries.8:13: Moses dresses Aaron's sons in their priestly clothes, just as God commanded. They too are being set apart to serve alongside their father.
entries.8:14: Moses brings the sin-offering ox, and Aaron and his sons lay their hands on its head. This gesture shows the people identifying with the animal that will bear their sin.
entries.8:15: Moses kills the ox and applies its blood to the altar to cleanse it. The blood is used to remove impurity so the altar can be used for holy service.
entries.8:16: Moses burns the fat parts of the inner organs on the altar. These choice parts are given to God as the offering's most valuable portion.
entries.8:17: The rest of the ox—skin, flesh, and waste—is burned outside the camp. This shows that what is unclean is removed from the community's holy space.
entries.8:18: Moses brings the first ram for the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons lay hands on it. Again they identify with the animal before it is offered.
entries.8:19: Moses kills the ram and puts its blood on and around the altar. The blood is central to making the offering acceptable to God.
entries.8:20: Moses cuts the ram into pieces and burns the head, parts, and fat. The offering is prepared carefully and completely for God.
entries.8:21: After washing the inner parts and legs, Moses burns the whole ram on the altar. The text calls it a pleasing smell to God, meaning the offering was accepted.
entries.8:22: Moses brings the second ram, the one for setting the priests apart, and Aaron and his sons lay hands on it. This offering is specifically for ordaining them to their role.
entries.8:23: Moses kills the ram and puts some of its blood on Aaron's right ear, thumb, and big toe. This symbolizes that Aaron's hearing, work, and walk are all dedicated to God.
entries.8:24: Moses does the same for Aaron's sons—blood on ear, thumb, and toe—and puts the rest on the altar. It shows the whole person is set apart for God's service.
entries.8:25: Moses takes the fat portions and the right leg of the ordination ram. These choice parts are prepared for the special offering.
entries.8:26: Moses takes three kinds of bread from the basket and places them on the fat and the leg. Bread is included in the offering, showing gratitude and fellowship with God.
entries.8:27: Moses places all these items in the hands of Aaron and his sons and waves them before God. The gesture presents the offering to God on behalf of the priests.
entries.8:28: Moses takes the offerings back from their hands and burns them on the altar. This completes the ordination offering as a pleasing smell to God.
entries.8:29: Moses waves the breast of the ram before God and keeps it as his own portion. This shows that those who serve God in this work are also provided for.
entries.8:30: Moses sprinkles oil and blood on Aaron, his sons, and their clothes to make them holy. This final act seals their dedication to God's service.
entries.8:31: Moses tells Aaron and his sons to cook and eat the meat and bread at the tent entrance. Eating the offering shows they share in what was given to God.
entries.8:32: Any leftover meat or bread must be burned, not kept. This teaches that what is holy is not to be treated as ordinary or wasted.
entries.8:33: Aaron and his sons must stay at the tent entrance for seven days while the ordination is completed. This period of waiting shows their full commitment to being set apart.
entries.8:34: Moses explains that everything done that day was commanded by God to take away sin. It reminds the reader that forgiveness comes on God's terms, not ours.
entries.8:35: The priests must guard the tent entrance day and night for seven days to avoid death. This shows how seriously God takes the holiness of his presence.
entries.8:36: Aaron and his sons do everything God commanded through Moses. Their obedience completes the ordination and shows the right response to God's instructions.
entries.9:1: This marks the start of Aaron's work as priest, eight days after he was set apart for the job. It shows that serving God begins with careful preparation and the right people present.
entries.9:2: Aaron is told to bring animals for two kinds of offerings, one to deal with sin and one given wholly to God. The animals had to be perfect, teaching that God deserves our best, not our leftovers.
entries.9:3: The people also bring their own offerings, including a goat for sin and perfect young animals to give to God. Everyone shares in this, showing that all people need forgiveness and a way to approach God.
entries.9:4: More animals are brought for a shared meal offering with God, along with grain mixed with oil. Moses tells them this is the day they will actually see the Lord show up, so they bring what He asked for.
entries.9:5: The people bring exactly what Moses commanded and gather at the entrance of the meeting tent, waiting expectantly. It pictures a community coming together, ready and watching for God to act.
entries.9:6: Moses tells them that doing what God commanded is the path to seeing His glory. Obedience comes first, and then God reveals Himself; we don't earn His presence, but we do prepare for it.
entries.9:7: Aaron must first offer for his own sin before he can serve on behalf of the people. Leaders need God's cleansing too, and no one stands before God on their own goodness.
entries.9:8: Aaron steps up to the altar and begins by killing the ox for his own sin offering. He starts with himself, showing that personal honesty before God comes before leading others.
entries.9:9: His sons hand him the blood, and he smears some on the altar's horns and pours the rest at its base. The blood stands for life given up to make things right with God.
entries.9:10: The rich parts of the animal are burned on the altar, just as God had instructed. Doing it exactly as commanded shows that worship is on God's terms, not ours.
entries.9:11: The parts not burned on the altar are taken outside the camp and burned. What couldn't be offered to God was removed from the community, keeping the holy and the ordinary separate.
entries.9:12: Aaron then kills the animal for the whole offering, and his sons bring him the blood to splash around the altar. This offering was given completely to God, a picture of total dedication.
entries.9:13: The pieces of the animal are handed to Aaron in order, including the head, and burned on the altar. The careful order shows that worship is done thoughtfully, not carelessly.
entries.9:14: The inner organs and legs are washed first, then burned with the rest of the offering. Even the hidden parts are cleaned and given to God, reminding us that He sees and wants our whole lives.
entries.9:15: Aaron now offers the people's sin offering, a goat, in the same way he did his own. The people's need for forgiveness is dealt with the same way as the priest's.
entries.9:16: He presents the people's whole offering according to the prescribed procedure. Following the pattern matters, because this is about obeying God rather than improvising.
entries.9:17: He brings the grain offering, burns a handful on the altar, and adds it to the morning offering. Daily worship builds on what was already given earlier that day.
entries.9:18: Aaron kills the ox and sheep for the people's peace offerings, and the blood is splashed around the altar. These offerings celebrated fellowship and peace with God, not just forgiveness.
entries.9:19: The fat portions of the animals are set aside, including the fat tail and the fat around the organs. The best and richest parts are reserved for God's altar.
entries.9:20: The fat is placed on the breasts and then burned on the altar. The priests handle the offering carefully, making sure God's portion is given to Him.
entries.9:21: Aaron lifts up the breast and right leg as a wave offering before the Lord, just as Moses ordered. Lifting the offering toward God was a physical way of saying it belongs to Him.
entries.9:22: After finishing the offerings, Aaron raises his hands and blesses the people, then steps down. The priest's job ends with words of blessing, sending the people home with God's favor.
entries.9:23: Moses and Aaron go into the meeting tent and come out blessing the people, and God's glory appears to everyone. When leaders and people obey, God's presence becomes visible to the whole community.
entries.9:24: Fire comes from God and consumes the offering on the altar, and the people cry out and fall face down. God Himself confirms the worship, and the people respond with awe and surrender.
entries.10:1: Two of Aaron's sons burned incense in a way God had not commanded. It means worship must be done God's way, not just however we think is best.
entries.10:2: Fire from God killed them on the spot. It shows that God takes disobedience in worship seriously, so we should approach him with respect.
entries.10:3: Moses tells Aaron that God will be treated as holy by those who come near him. It means God deserves honor from those who serve him, and Aaron quietly accepted this.
entries.10:4: Moses had two relatives carry the bodies away from the holy area. It means the dead bodies had to be removed from the sacred place to keep it clean.
entries.10:5: The two men did exactly what Moses said and carried the bodies out. It shows they obeyed quickly and carefully.
entries.10:6: Moses told Aaron and his remaining sons not to show public mourning, so they would not also die. It means their role as priests came first, while the rest of the people could grieve.
entries.10:7: They were told to stay at the entrance of the meeting tent because they had been set apart with holy oil. It means their special service to God required them to stay at their post.
entries.10:8: God spoke directly to Aaron here. It sets up the instruction that follows for him and his sons.
entries.10:9: Priests were forbidden to drink wine or strong drink before entering the meeting tent. It means they needed clear minds to serve God, and this rule was to last for all generations.
entries.10:10: Priests had to tell the difference between what is holy and common, and between clean and unclean. It means God's people need clear guidance about what honors him and what does not.
entries.10:11: The priests were to teach the people all the laws God gave through Moses. It means part of serving God is teaching others what he has said.
entries.10:12: Moses told the surviving sons to eat the rest of the grain offering beside the altar. It means the priests were to receive this most holy food in the proper place.
entries.10:13: This food was to be eaten in a holy place as the priests' rightful share. It means God provided for those who served him at the altar.
entries.10:14: The breast and thigh from the peace offerings were for the priests and their families to eat in a clean place. It means God's provision extended to the priests' households.
entries.10:15: The breast and thigh were to be presented before the Lord along with the fat. It means these portions were set apart for the priests and their descendants permanently.
entries.10:16: Moses looked for the goat of the sin offering and found it had been burned up, and he was angry with the two remaining sons. It means he expected the proper procedure to be followed.
entries.10:17: Moses asked why they had not eaten the sin offering in the holy place. It means this meal was part of how the people's sin was dealt with before God.
entries.10:18: Since the blood was not brought into the holy place, the meat should have been eaten there. It means Moses was pointing out that the rules had not been followed.
entries.10:19: Aaron explained that with such tragedy happening that day, eating the offering would not have been right. It means he was asking whether God would really have been pleased with that.
entries.10:20: When Moses heard Aaron's reasoning, he accepted it and stopped being angry. It means Moses was willing to listen and reconsider when given a good explanation.
entries.11:1: God speaks here to Moses and Aaron, the leaders of Israel, giving them instructions to pass on. It shows that God guides his people through chosen leaders.
entries.11:2: God tells the Israelites which animals they are allowed to eat. This was a way of setting his people apart from the nations around them.
entries.11:3: An animal could be eaten if it chewed its food twice over and had a split hoof. These were the marks that made it acceptable food for Israel.
entries.11:4: The camel chews its food twice over but does not have a split hoof, so it was not to be eaten. It was off-limits for God's people.
entries.11:5: The rock-badger was also not to be eaten because it did not have a split hoof. It was treated as unclean for Israel.
entries.11:6: The hare was not to be eaten because its foot was not split in two. It too was unclean for the people.
entries.11:7: The pig has a split hoof but does not chew its food twice over, so it was not to be eaten. It was unclean for Israel.
entries.11:8: The people were not to eat these animals or even touch their dead bodies. Touching them would make a person unclean and unfit for worship.
entries.11:9: Water creatures could be eaten if they had fins and scales. These were the signs of clean food from the water.
entries.11:10: Any water creature without fins and scales was to be avoided. It was considered unfit and disgusting for food.
entries.11:11: Such creatures were not to be eaten, and their dead bodies were to be avoided. They were treated as unfit for God's people.
entries.11:12: Anything in the water without fins and scales was off-limits. The people were to treat it as unfit for food.
entries.11:13: Certain birds, starting with eagles and ospreys, were not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit food for Israel.
entries.11:14: Kites and falcons and similar birds were also on the list of birds not to be eaten. They were unclean for the people.
entries.11:15: Ravens and similar birds were not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit food for Israel.
entries.11:16: Ostriches, night-hawks, sea-hawks, and similar birds were not to be eaten. They were unclean for the people.
entries.11:17: Little owls, cormorants, and great owls were among the birds not to be eaten. They were off-limits as food.
entries.11:18: Water-hens, pelicans, and vultures were also not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit for God's people.
entries.11:19: Storks, herons, hoopoes, and bats were not to be eaten. They were unclean for Israel.
entries.11:20: Winged creatures that walk on four legs were to be avoided as food. They were considered unfit for the people.
entries.11:21: Some winged creatures with four legs could be eaten if they had long legs for jumping. These were the exception to the rule.
entries.11:22: Locusts of various kinds were allowed as food. They were the clean exception among jumping winged creatures.
entries.11:23: All other winged four-legged creatures were not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit for God's people.
entries.11:24: Touching the dead body of these creatures made a person unclean until evening. This meant they could not take part in worship until they were clean again.
entries.11:25: Anyone who carried away such a dead body had to wash their clothes and stay unclean until evening. Cleansing required both washing and waiting.
entries.11:26: Animals without a fully split hoof or that do not chew their food twice over were unclean. Touching them made a person unclean.
entries.11:27: Four-footed animals that walk on the pads of their feet were unclean. Touching their dead bodies made a person unclean until evening.
entries.11:28: Carrying away the dead body of such an animal required washing clothes and being unclean until evening. The person was restored to cleanliness after that.
entries.11:29: Small creatures that move low on the ground, like weasels, mice, and large lizards, were unclean. They were not to be eaten or touched.
entries.11:30: Ferrets, land crocodiles, lizards, sand-lizards, and chameleons were also unclean. They were off-limits for God's people.
entries.11:31: Touching these creatures when dead made a person unclean until evening. They could not worship until they were clean again.
entries.11:32: If a dead body of these creatures fell on something, that object became unclean. Wood, clothing, skin, or bags had to be put in water and were unclean until evening.
entries.11:33: If such a dead body fell into a clay pot, everything inside became unclean and the pot had to be broken. Clay pots could not be cleaned, so they were destroyed.
entries.11:34: Food or drink that came from such an unclean pot became unclean too. Uncleanness spread from the pot to what was in it.
entries.11:35: If a dead body fell on an oven or cooking pot, it had to be broken. These items became unclean and could not be used.
entries.11:36: A spring or a water storage place stayed clean even if a dead body touched it. But anyone who touched the dead body was still unclean.
entries.11:37: If a dead body fell on seed for planting, the seed stayed clean. Dry seed was not affected by uncleanness.
entries.11:38: But if the seed had been soaked in water and a dead body touched it, the seed became unclean. Water made the seed able to receive uncleanness.
entries.11:39: If an animal allowed for food died on its own, anyone who touched its body was unclean until evening. Natural death made even clean animals unfit to touch.
entries.11:40: Anyone who ate from such a dead animal or carried its body had to wash their clothes and stay unclean until evening. Cleansing required washing and waiting until evening.
entries.11:41: Small creatures that move along the ground were not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit food for Israel.
entries.11:42: Creatures that crawl on their belly, on four legs, or on many legs were not to be eaten. They were all considered unfit for God's people.
entries.11:43: The people were told not to make themselves unclean by these creatures. They were to stay set apart and not become unfit through contact with them.
entries.11:44: God says he is the Lord their God, so they must set themselves apart and be holy. Being holy means living differently because they belong to him.
entries.11:45: God brought Israel out of Egypt to be their God, so they must be holy as he is holy. Their conduct was to reflect the God who rescued them.
entries.11:46: This verse summarizes the whole set of rules about animals, birds, and water creatures. It shows the teaching covered every kind of creature the people might meet.
entries.11:47: The rules were meant to teach the difference between clean and unclean, and between animals that could and could not be eaten. God's people were to know and follow that difference.
entries.12:1: God speaks these instructions directly to Moses, showing that what follows is meant to be passed on to the people as God's guidance. For the reader, it reminds us that these rules come from God and were given for a reason.
entries.12:2: After a woman gives birth to a boy, she is considered ritually unclean for seven days, much like during her monthly period. This was about ceremonial purity in worship, not about the baby or birth being wrong.
entries.12:3: On the eighth day the baby boy is to be circumcised. This was the physical sign of God's covenant with Israel, marking the child as part of God's people.
entries.12:4: The mother then waits thirty-three more days while her bleeding stops, and during this time she cannot touch sacred things or enter the holy place. This set a period of rest and separation before she could return to full worship.
entries.12:5: If the baby is a girl, the waiting periods are doubled, two weeks plus sixty-six days. The text simply states this rule without explaining why, and it reflects the cultural setting of that time.
entries.12:6: When her waiting period ends, the mother brings a young lamb as a burned offering and a pigeon or dove as a sin offering to the priest at the entrance of the meeting tent. These offerings marked her return to worship and dealt with any ritual impurity.
entries.12:7: The priest offers these sacrifices to God to make atonement for her, and she is declared clean from her bleeding. This gave the woman a clear, official way to be restored to full participation in worship.
entries.12:8: If she cannot afford a lamb, she may bring two doves or two young pigeons instead, and the priest makes atonement so she is clean. God made provision for poorer families, so no one was excluded from being restored.
entries.13:1: God is giving instructions to Moses and Aaron, the leaders and priests of Israel. This shows that caring for the health of the community was part of their God-given responsibility.
entries.13:2: If someone notices a swelling, rash, or bright spot on their skin that might be a serious skin disease, they were to be brought to the priest to be examined. The priest, not a doctor, served as the one who checked and decided the person's status in the community.
entries.13:3: The priest looks for signs that the problem is serious: white hair in the spot and the sore going deeper than the skin. If those signs are there, the priest declares the person unclean, meaning they must be separated from others for a time.
entries.13:4: If the spot looks minor and the signs aren't clear, the priest doesn't decide right away but has the person stay apart for seven days to see what happens. This teaches patience rather than rushing to judgment.
entries.13:5: After a week the priest checks again, and if the spot hasn't gotten worse or spread, the person waits another seven days. Careful watching protects both the sick person and the community.
entries.13:6: If after the second week the spot has faded and not spread, the priest declares the person clean, and they wash their clothes and return to normal life. This gave people a clear way back into the community.
entries.13:7: If the spot spreads after the person was examined, they must go back to the priest for another look. A change for the worse means the matter needs to be rechecked.
entries.13:8: If the priest sees the spot has spread, he declares the person unclean because it is a real skin disease. The spreading is the key sign that this is serious.
entries.13:9: Whenever a serious skin disease appears on someone, they are to be brought to the priest. The priest again serves as the one who confirms what is happening.
entries.13:10: The priest checks for a white swelling, white hair, and raw, open flesh in the sore. These are signs that the disease is active and serious.
entries.13:11: If these signs show the disease is long-standing, the priest declares the person unclean right away without waiting. Clear evidence means no need for further testing.
entries.13:12: If the disease has spread over the person's whole skin, from head to foot, as far as the priest can see, the situation is examined as a whole. The priest looks at the total picture, not just one spot.
entries.13:13: If the priest sees that the whole body has turned white, he declares the person clean, because the skin has fully changed and is no longer raw and open. In this case, the complete whitening is actually a good sign.
entries.13:14: But if raw, open flesh appears anywhere on the person, that is a sign of uncleanness. Open, diseased flesh is the real problem, not just the color of the skin.
entries.13:15: When the priest sees raw flesh, he declares the person unclean, because open diseased flesh means the disease is active. The visible condition, not rumor or fear, decides the outcome.
entries.13:16: If the raw flesh heals and turns white again, the person is to come back to the priest. Healing is possible, and the person is not permanently shut out.
entries.13:17: If the priest sees that the spot has turned white, he declares the person clean and free of the disease. The priest's confirmation restores the person to the community.
entries.13:18: This covers the case of a boil or sore on the skin that has healed. Even after healing, the area needs to be checked if something new appears there.
entries.13:19: If a white swelling or a reddish-white bright spot appears where the boil was, the priest must examine it. A new mark in an old wound could be a sign of something serious.
entries.13:20: If the spot goes deeper than the skin and the hair in it has turned white, the priest declares the person unclean because the disease has started in the old sore. The location doesn't change the seriousness of the signs.
entries.13:21: If the priest sees no white hair, the spot isn't deep, and it isn't bright, he has the person stay apart for seven days. When signs are unclear, waiting and watching is the wise response.
entries.13:22: If the spot spreads during that week, the priest declares the person unclean because it is a real disease. Spreading confirms the problem.
entries.13:23: If the bright spot stays the same size and doesn't spread, it is just the scar from the old wound, and the priest declares the person clean. Not every mark is a disease.
entries.13:24: This covers a burn on the skin where the burned flesh becomes a bright reddish-white or white spot. Burns, like other wounds, need to be checked for signs of disease.
entries.13:25: If the hair in the bright spot has turned white and the spot goes deeper than the skin, the priest declares the person unclean because the disease has started in the burn. The same signs mean the same conclusion, wherever they appear.
entries.13:26: If the priest sees no white hair, the spot isn't deep, and it isn't bright, he has the person stay apart for seven days. Again, unclear cases are watched rather than decided quickly.
entries.13:27: If on the seventh day the spot has spread, the priest declares the person unclean because it is a real disease. Spreading is the deciding sign.
entries.13:28: If the bright spot stays the same size, doesn't spread, and fades, it is just the mark of the burn, and the priest declares the person clean. A healing burn scar is not a disease.
entries.13:29: This begins a new case: a disease on the head or in the hair of the chin, affecting a man or a woman. Problems in hair-covered areas needed their own careful examination.
entries.13:30: If the priest sees the sore goes deeper than the skin and has thin yellow hair in it, he declares the person unclean because it is a serious skin disease. Yellow, thin hair is a warning sign.
entries.13:31: If the sore doesn't seem deep and there is no black hair in it, the priest has the person stay apart for seven days. Lack of clear signs means watch and wait.
entries.13:32: On the seventh day the priest checks again: if the sore hasn't spread, has no yellow hair, and isn't deep, it still isn't confirmed. The examination continues until the signs are clear.
entries.13:33: The person shaves their hair except over the sore, and stays apart for another seven days. Shaving helps the priest see the sore clearly without cutting into the diseased area.
entries.13:34: If on the seventh day the sore hasn't spread and isn't deep, the priest declares the person clean, and after washing their clothes they return to normal life. Clear results mean a clear return to the community.
entries.13:35: If the disease gets worse after the person was declared clean, the matter must be looked at again. A clean verdict isn't the end of the story if things change.
entries.13:36: If the priest sees the sore has spread, he declares the person unclean without even checking for yellow hair. Spreading alone is enough to confirm the disease.
entries.13:37: If the sore has stopped spreading and black hair has grown in it, the disease is gone, and the priest declares the person clean. New, normal hair is a sign of healing.
entries.13:38: This covers bright white marks on the skin of a man or a woman. Not every white mark is serious, so each case is examined.
entries.13:39: If the white marks are not very bright, it is only a harmless skin condition, and the priest declares the person clean. Mild skin problems don't make a person unclean.
entries.13:40: If a man loses his hair and becomes bald, he is still clean. Baldness is not a disease and doesn't affect a person's standing in the community.
entries.13:41: Losing hair at the front of the head is just normal baldness, not a sickness, so the person is still considered clean. This means you don't need to worry that ordinary baldness makes you unfit.
entries.13:42: But if a reddish-white sore appears on a bald head or forehead, that is a serious skin disease breaking out. It means a real problem can show up even where there is no hair, so it should be checked.
entries.13:43: When the priest examines it and the sore on the bald area looks reddish-white like a serious skin disease, he must treat it as such. The point is that the priest carefully inspects before deciding anything.
entries.13:44: The priest must declare that person unclean, because the disease is on his head. This means the priest's verdict mattered, and the person had to be treated as unclean for everyone's safety.
entries.13:45: A person with this disease had to show signs of mourning, leave his hair loose, cover his mouth, and shout that he was unclean. This means he had to warn others to stay away and live openly as someone in sorrow.
entries.13:46: As long as the disease lasted, the person had to live alone outside the camp. This means he was separated from the community to protect others from infection.
entries.13:47: The same rules applied to clothing made of wool or linen that showed signs of disease. This means the concern for uncleanness wasn't only about people but also about their belongings.
entries.13:48: The rules covered anything woven from linen or wool, and also leather and items made from skin. This means even everyday materials had to be checked for spreading damage.
entries.13:49: If reddish or greenish marks appeared on cloth or leather, it was treated as a serious spreading disease, and the priest had to inspect it. This means suspicious spots on belongings were taken seriously, not ignored.
entries.13:50: After the priest looked at the marked item, it was set aside for seven days. This means they waited to see whether the problem would spread before deciding what to do.
entries.13:51: On the seventh day the priest checked again, and if the mark had spread, the item was declared unclean as a damaging disease. This means spreading damage showed the problem was serious.
entries.13:52: The clothing or leather with the spreading disease had to be burned up completely. This means the item was destroyed so the contamination could not continue.
entries.13:53: But if the priest saw that the mark had not spread on the cloth or leather, he did not condemn it yet. This means not every spot meant destruction; they checked carefully first.
entries.13:54: The priest then ordered the item to be washed and set aside for another seven days. This means they gave it a fair chance to be cleaned before deciding.
entries.13:55: If the mark stayed the same color and had not spread even after washing, the item still had to be burned, because the damage was working through it. This means washing alone doesn't fix a problem that has gotten into the material.
entries.13:56: If the mark faded after washing, the priest had that spot cut out of the cloth or leather. This means removing the damaged part could save the rest of the item.
entries.13:57: If the mark came back on the clothing or leather, it was a disease breaking out again, and the item had to be burned. This means a problem that keeps returning is serious and must be dealt with fully.
entries.13:58: If the item was washed and the mark was gone, it was washed once more and then counted clean. This means careful cleaning could restore something that had been in doubt.
entries.13:59: This sums up the rules for judging whether clothing or leather with a mark was clean or unclean. This means God gave clear guidelines so the priests could make fair and consistent decisions.
entries.14:1: God is speaking directly to Moses, giving him instructions to pass on to the people. This shows that what follows is God's own direction, not just human custom.
entries.14:2: This begins the rules for what happens when a person with a serious skin disease is healed and wants to be declared clean again. The person goes to the priest, who serves as the one who confirms the healing.
entries.14:3: The priest goes outside the camp to examine the person, since the sick person had been kept away from the community. If the disease is clearly gone, the healing is confirmed.
entries.14:4: The priest orders certain items for the cleansing ceremony: two live birds, cedar wood, red thread, and a plant called hyssop. These were common materials used in rituals of cleansing.
entries.14:5: One bird is killed in a clay pot over fresh running water. The running water likely stands for life and purity in the ceremony.
entries.14:6: The living bird, along with the wood, thread, and hyssop, is dipped into the dead bird's blood mixed with water. The living bird represents the person being restored to life and community.
entries.14:7: The priest sprinkles the person seven times, declares them clean, and releases the living bird into the open field. The freed bird pictures the person being set free from their isolation.
entries.14:8: The healed person washes their clothes, shaves, and bathes, then may return to the camp but must stay outside their own tent for seven days. Cleansing was gradual, showing that full restoration took time.
entries.14:9: On the seventh day the person shaves off all hair and washes again. Removing all hair made sure nothing unclean remained, and then they were fully clean.
entries.14:10: On the eighth day the person brings animals and grain offerings for the formal ceremony. These were costly gifts given to complete the cleansing before God.
entries.14:11: The priest presents the person and their offerings at the entrance of the meeting tent, the place of worship. This brings the healed person back before God and the community.
entries.14:12: The priest offers one male lamb and the oil as a special offering waved before the Lord. The waving was a way of dedicating the gift to God.
entries.14:13: The lamb is killed in the same holy place where sin and burnt offerings were made. The offering is treated as very holy and belongs to the priest.
entries.14:14: Some of the blood is put on the person's right ear, right thumb, and right big toe. This marked the person's hearing, working, and walking as set apart for God.
entries.14:15: The priest pours some of the oil into his own left hand. The oil is used alongside the blood in the cleansing ritual.
entries.14:16: The priest dips his right finger in the oil and sprinkles it seven times before the Lord. The number seven signals completeness in the cleansing.
entries.14:17: More oil is placed on the same spots as the blood: ear, thumb, and toe. The oil goes over the blood, showing cleansing layered on top of the offering.
entries.14:18: The remaining oil is poured on the person's head, and the priest makes them right with God. The oil on the head marks the person as restored and blessed.
entries.14:19: The priest then offers the sin offering to deal with the person's uncleanness, followed by the burnt offering. Both offerings were needed to fully restore the person before God.
entries.14:20: The burnt offering and grain offering are burned on the altar, and the priest makes the person clean. The ceremony ends with the person fully restored.
entries.14:21: A poor person who cannot afford the full set may bring a smaller offering. God made room for people of little means to be cleansed too.
entries.14:22: Instead of larger animals, the poor person may bring two doves or pigeons, one for each offering. This shows God's care for those who cannot pay full price.
entries.14:23: On the eighth day the person brings these offerings to the priest at the meeting tent. The timing and place are the same as for the wealthier person.
entries.14:24: The priest takes the lamb and the oil and waves them before the Lord. This dedicates the gifts to God on behalf of the poor person.
entries.14:25: The lamb is killed and its blood is put on the person's right ear, thumb, and big toe, just as in the fuller ceremony. The poor person receives the same marking as anyone else.
entries.14:26: The priest pours some oil into his left hand. The oil ritual continues exactly as before.
entries.14:27: The priest sprinkles oil with his right finger seven times before the Lord. This repeats the sign of complete cleansing.
entries.14:28: Oil is placed on the ear, thumb, and toe, right where the blood was put. The same spots are marked with both blood and oil.
entries.14:29: The rest of the oil goes on the person's head to make them right with God. The poor person's cleansing is just as complete as the rich person's.
entries.14:30: The priest offers one of the doves or pigeons the person was able to bring. The offering matches what the person can afford.
entries.14:31: One bird is the sin offering and the other the burnt offering, along with the grain offering. The priest then makes the person clean before the Lord.
entries.14:32: This sums up the rules for a person with skin disease who is too poor to afford the usual offerings. God provided a way for everyone to be restored.
entries.14:33: God now speaks to both Moses and Aaron, since Aaron and the priests will carry out these rules. The instructions that follow are for life in the promised land.
entries.14:34: God says that when the people enter Canaan, he may allow a spreading mildew-like condition to appear in a house. Even problems in buildings are under God's notice.
entries.14:35: The owner of the house reports the problem to the priest, describing it as something like a skin disease in the house. The priest is the one who inspects it.
entries.14:36: Before the priest goes in, everything is taken out of the house so the belongings don't become unclean. The inspection is done carefully to limit the damage.
entries.14:37: If the priest sees green or red hollow spots that seem to go deeper than the wall's surface, the problem is serious. These signs showed the house was contaminated.
entries.14:38: The priest leaves and shuts up the house for seven days. A waiting period was used to see whether the problem would spread.
entries.14:39: The priest returns on the seventh day and checks whether the spots have grown. Spreading marks meant the problem was active and needed action.
entries.14:40: If the marks have spread, the priest orders the affected stones removed and thrown in an unclean place outside town. The contaminated parts had to be taken out to protect the rest.
entries.14:41: The inside of the house is scraped all around, and the scraped dust is dumped outside town in an unclean place. This removed any remaining contamination from the walls.
entries.14:42: New stones are put in place of the old ones, and the house is re-plastered. The house is repaired and made whole again.
entries.14:43: If the marks come back after the stones were removed and the house re-plastered, the problem is still active. A return of the disease meant the repair had failed.
entries.14:44: The priest then declares the house unclean because the mark is spreading and cannot be cured. The whole house is treated as contaminated.
entries.14:45: The house must be torn down, and its stones, wood, and plaster are carried outside town to an unclean place. A house that could not be cleansed had to be destroyed.
entries.14:46: Anyone who goes into the house while it is shut up becomes unclean until evening. Contact with the contaminated house made a person ritually unclean for the day.
entries.14:47: Anyone who sleeps or eats in the house must wash their clothes. Even indirect contact with the house required cleansing.
entries.14:48: If the priest sees that the marks have not spread after the house was re-plastered, he declares it clean because the problem is gone. The house is restored to normal use.
entries.14:49: To cleanse the house, the priest takes two birds, cedar wood, red thread, and hyssop, the same items used for a person. The house receives a ceremony like the one for a healed person.
entries.14:50: One bird is killed over fresh running water in a clay pot. This mirrors the ritual used for cleansing a person.
entries.14:51: The living bird, wood, thread, and hyssop are dipped in the blood and water, and the house is sprinkled seven times. The sprinkling marks the house as cleansed.
entries.14:52: The priest uses the bird, water, wood, thread, and hyssop to make the house right with God. The same elements that cleansed a person now cleanse the building.
entries.14:53: The living bird is released into the open field, and the house is declared clean. The freed bird pictures the contamination being carried away.
entries.14:54: This begins a summary of all the rules about skin disease and mildew. The laws covered both people and houses.
entries.14:55: The rules apply to skin disease on people and to mildew or contamination in clothing and houses. God's concern for cleanliness reached every part of daily life.
entries.14:56: The rules also cover swellings, rashes, and bright spots on the skin. These were the various signs the priest had to examine.
entries.14:57: These laws taught the people how to tell what was unclean and what was clean. Knowing the difference helped them live safely and worship God properly.
entries.15:1: God is speaking here, giving instructions to both Moses and Aaron, the leader and the priest. It shows that these rules about ritual purity were meant to guide the whole community's worship.
entries.15:2: A man with an unusual discharge from his body was considered ritually unclean under Israel's purity laws. For the reader, this shows that ancient Israel treated bodily conditions as matters of ritual status, not personal guilt.
entries.15:3: Whether the discharge kept flowing or was blocked, the man stayed unclean either way. The point is that the condition itself, not its severity, determined his ritual status.
entries.15:4: Anything the man lay on or sat on became unclean too. This shows how uncleanness in these laws spread through contact to everyday objects.
entries.15:5: Anyone who touched his bed had to wash their clothes and body and stayed unclean until evening. This taught Israel that contact with uncleanness required cleansing and a waiting period.
entries.15:6: Sitting where the unclean man had sat made a person unclean until evening, with washing required. The lesson is that uncleanness spread through ordinary contact and had to be dealt with.
entries.15:7: Touching the man's body directly made a person unclean until evening, requiring washing. This reinforced that physical contact with the unclean condition carried ritual consequences.
entries.15:8: If the unclean man spat on someone clean, that person became unclean until evening and had to wash. Even small contact could spread ritual uncleanness under these laws.
entries.15:9: A saddle or leather seat the unclean man rode on became unclean. This shows the rules extended to everyday items like riding gear.
entries.15:10: Touching anything that had been under the man made a person unclean until evening, and carrying such items required washing. The laws treated uncleanness as something that clung to objects and people.
entries.15:11: If the unclean man touched someone without having washed his hands, that person became unclean until evening and had to wash. Handwashing mattered because uncleanness could pass on through touch.
entries.15:12: A clay jar he touched had to be broken, while a wooden one could be washed. Porous clay could not be cleansed, so it was destroyed, showing how seriously these laws treated contamination.
entries.15:13: Once the discharge stopped, the man waited seven days, washed his clothes, and bathed in fresh running water to become clean. Full restoration required time, washing, and running water.
entries.15:14: On the eighth day he brought two doves or pigeons to the priest at the entrance of the meeting tent. The person did not approach God empty-handed but came with an offering.
entries.15:15: The priest offered one bird as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering to make atonement for the man. This shows that becoming clean again involved both washing and a sacrifice before God.
entries.15:16: A man's normal emission of semen made him unclean until evening, and he had to bathe. Even ordinary bodily functions were treated as requiring ritual cleansing.
entries.15:17: Clothing or leather that the semen touched had to be washed and stayed unclean until evening. The laws applied to everyday items, not just to people.
entries.15:18: When a man and woman had sexual relations, both had to bathe and were unclean until evening. This treated normal married intimacy as a temporary ritual state, not as sin.
entries.15:19: A woman's monthly bleeding made her ritually separate for seven days, and anyone who touched her was unclean until evening. This was a ritual status, not a moral judgment on her.
entries.15:20: Anything she lay on or sat on during her separation became unclean. Her ordinary furniture and resting places were affected by her ritual state.
entries.15:21: Touching her bed required washing clothes and body and left a person unclean until evening. Contact with her ritual uncleanness had to be cleansed.
entries.15:22: Touching anything she had sat on made a person unclean until evening, requiring washing. The same rule applied to her seating as to her bed.
entries.15:23: Anyone touching her bed or seat was unclean until evening. The uncleanness attached to those objects and passed to whoever touched them.
entries.15:24: If a man had sex with her during her period, he became unclean for seven days, and his bed became unclean too. This carried a heavier consequence than ordinary contact.
