entries.15:25: If a woman bled for many days outside her normal cycle, she stayed unclean as long as the bleeding lasted. The law covered irregular and prolonged conditions, not just the usual monthly pattern.
entries.15:26: During that long flow, her bed and seat were unclean just as during her normal period. The same rules applied to her furniture in both cases.
entries.15:27: Anyone touching those things became unclean until evening and had to wash. Contact with her uncleanness required cleansing, as in the normal case.
entries.15:28: When her bleeding stopped, she waited seven days, and then she was clean. Restoration came after the condition ended and a set period passed.
entries.15:29: On the eighth day she brought two doves or pigeons to the priest at the meeting tent. Like the man, she came with an offering to complete her cleansing.
entries.15:30: The priest offered one bird as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering to make atonement for her. Her cleansing was completed before God through sacrifice.
entries.15:31: God gave these rules to keep Israel from defiling his holy dwelling place and to protect them from death. The laws were about guarding worship, not about shaming people for bodily functions.
entries.15:32: This verse summarizes the law for a man with a discharge or a normal emission that made him unclean. It introduces the closing summary of the chapter's rules.
entries.15:33: The summary also covers a woman's bleeding, any unclean discharge, and a man who has relations with a woman during her period. These rules applied to both men and women and to intimate situations.
entries.16:1: God spoke to Moses right after Aaron's two sons died for approaching God in a way he had not commanded. It reminds the reader that God takes worship seriously.
entries.16:2: God told Moses to warn Aaron not to enter the most holy inner room whenever he liked, because God's presence there could kill him. It shows that coming near to God is not casual.
entries.16:3: Aaron could only enter that holy place by bringing the required sacrifices, a bull for sin and a ram for a burnt offering. It teaches that approaching God requires the right offering.
entries.16:4: Aaron had to wear simple holy linen clothes and wash his body before entering. It shows that those who come before God must be cleansed and set apart.
entries.16:5: The people were to supply two male goats for a sin offering and one ram for a burnt offering. It shows the whole community shared in the cost of dealing with sin.
entries.16:6: Aaron first offered a bull to cover his own sins and his family's sins. It reminds the reader that leaders too need forgiveness before serving others.
entries.16:7: Aaron brought the two goats and presented them before the Lord at the entrance of the meeting tent. It shows that the ritual was done openly before God, not in secret.
entries.16:8: Aaron cast lots to decide which goat belonged to the Lord and which was for Azazel, the scapegoat. It shows that God himself directed how sin would be dealt with.
entries.16:9: The goat chosen for the Lord was sacrificed as a sin offering. It pictures sin being dealt with through a life given up.
entries.16:10: The other goat was kept alive and sent into the wilderness to carry away the people's sin. It pictures sin being removed far away, not just covered.
entries.16:11: Aaron sacrificed his own bull to make atonement for himself and his household. It shows that even the high priest needed cleansing before he could help others.
entries.16:12: Aaron took burning coals and crushed incense from the altar into the most holy place. It shows careful preparation was required to enter God's presence.
entries.16:13: The incense smoke covered the ark so Aaron would not die when he came near God's presence. It shows God's mercy in shielding a sinful man from his holiness.
entries.16:14: Aaron sprinkled some of the bull's blood on and in front of the ark's cover seven times. It pictures blood being applied to make atonement before God.
entries.16:15: Aaron then killed the people's sin-offering goat and sprinkled its blood in the same way inside the veil. It shows the people's sin was dealt with at the very center of worship.
entries.16:16: Aaron cleansed the holy place from the people's uncleanness and wrongdoing, and did the same for the meeting tent among them. It shows sin contaminates even sacred space and needs cleansing.
entries.16:17: No one else was allowed in the meeting tent while Aaron made atonement until he came out. It shows atonement was a solemn, solitary work done before God alone.
entries.16:18: Aaron then cleansed the altar by putting blood on its horns and around it. It shows that even the place of sacrifice needed to be made clean.
entries.16:19: Aaron sprinkled blood on the altar seven times to make it holy and clean from the people's uncleanness. It pictures thorough cleansing by blood.
entries.16:20: After cleansing the holy place, the meeting tent, and the altar, Aaron brought the live goat forward. It shows the removal of sin followed the cleansing of sin.
entries.16:21: Aaron laid both hands on the live goat, confessed the people's sins over it, and sent it into the wilderness. It pictures the people's guilt being placed on another and carried away.
entries.16:22: The goat carried all their sins into a desolate land far from people. It shows sin being taken away completely, not left hanging over them.
entries.16:23: Aaron took off the special linen clothes in the meeting tent after finishing the holy place ritual. It shows a clear ending to the sacred work before returning to normal duties.
entries.16:24: Aaron washed, put his regular clothes back on, and offered burnt offerings for himself and the people. It shows cleansing and offering continued until sin was fully dealt with.
entries.16:25: Aaron burned the fat of the sin offering on the altar. It shows the offering was completed as God had instructed.
entries.16:26: The man who led the scapegoat away had to wash his clothes and body before returning to camp. It shows contact with sin, even symbolically, required cleansing.
entries.16:27: The bodies of the sin-offering animals whose blood was used were burned outside the camp. It shows sin was taken outside the community, away from God's people.
entries.16:28: The man who burned those bodies also had to wash before coming back to camp. It reinforces that handling sin's remains made a person unclean.
entries.16:29: God made this an ongoing yearly command: on the tenth day of the seventh month the people were to humble themselves and do no work. It shows a regular day set aside for dealing with sin.
entries.16:30: On that day their sin was taken away and they were made clean before the Lord. It shows God provided a real, repeated way for his people to be forgiven.
entries.16:31: It was to be a special Sabbath of rest and self-denial, a lasting rule. It teaches that receiving forgiveness calls for humble, unhurried attention to God.
entries.16:32: The anointed high priest who succeeded Aaron was to perform this atonement work wearing the holy linen clothes. It shows God set apart a specific person to lead this cleansing.
entries.16:33: He was to cleanse the holy place, the meeting tent, the altar, the priests, and all the people. It shows atonement reached every part of the community's life.
entries.16:34: This yearly atonement was a lasting command, and Moses did exactly as the Lord ordered. It shows God's people were to keep obeying his instructions for forgiveness year after year.
entries.17:1: God is speaking directly to Moses, giving him instructions to pass on. This reminds the reader that these rules come from God himself, not from human invention.
entries.17:2: Moses is told to deliver God's command to the priests and to the whole community of Israel. Everyone is expected to hear and follow it, not just the religious leaders.
entries.17:3: This rule covers any Israelite who kills an ox, sheep, or goat, whether inside the camp or out in the open. It sets the scene for where such killing must be done.
entries.17:4: If someone kills an animal for sacrifice but doesn't bring it to the entrance of the meeting tent, he is guilty of taking a life and must be removed from the community. The point is that worship must go through the place and way God appointed, not wherever a person chooses.
entries.17:5: The purpose is that Israelites stop killing animals out in the open fields and instead bring them to the priest at the meeting tent as peace offerings to the Lord. It moves their worship from private, scattered practice to the one place God designated.
entries.17:6: The priest splashes the blood on God's altar at the tent entrance and burns the fat as a pleasing offering. This shows that the priest handles the sacred parts of the sacrifice on the people's behalf.
entries.17:7: The people must stop sacrificing to evil spirits, which they had been chasing after instead of God. This is to be a permanent rule for all their generations, showing that divided loyalty to false powers is never acceptable.
entries.17:8: This applies to any Israelite or foreigner living among them who brings a burnt offering or any other sacrifice. The rule is stated broadly so no one can claim it doesn't apply to them.
entries.17:9: If such a person doesn't bring the offering to the entrance of the meeting tent, he must be cut off from his people. Worship offered on one's own terms, apart from God's appointed place, is treated as a serious offense.
entries.17:10: God says he will personally set himself against anyone, Israelite or foreigner, who eats blood, and that person will be cut off from the community. This shows how seriously God treats the eating of blood.
entries.17:11: The reason is that the life of a creature is in its blood, and God has given blood on the altar to deal with sin. Blood cleanses from sin because it carries the life that is being offered.
entries.17:12: Because blood is the life and is set apart for atonement, God forbids anyone in the community, including foreigners, from eating it. The reader is reminded that this is not a minor dietary rule but something tied to the sacredness of life.
entries.17:13: Anyone who hunts an animal or bird for food must pour out its blood and cover it with earth. This treats the creature's life with respect rather than letting its blood be casually consumed.
entries.17:14: Again the reason is given: the blood is the life of every creature, so no one may eat it, and anyone who does will be cut off. The repeated warning shows how central this principle is.
entries.17:15: Anyone, native or foreigner, who eats an animal that died on its own or was killed by another animal must wash their clothes and bathe, staying unclean until evening, then they are clean. This shows that even accidental contact with improper food requires cleansing.
entries.17:16: If the person refuses to wash and bathe, they carry the guilt of their sin. The reader learns that ignoring God's cleansing requirement leaves a person accountable, not merely unclean.
entries.18:1: God is speaking directly to Moses, the leader of the Israelites. This sets up the instructions that follow as coming from God himself.
entries.18:2: God reminds the people that he is their God, so what he says carries authority over their lives. The reader is meant to hear this as a call to take God's words personally.
entries.18:3: God tells the Israelites not to copy the sexual and social customs of Egypt, where they used to live, or of Canaan, where they are going. Your past and your surroundings should not decide how you live.
entries.18:4: Instead of following other cultures, the people are to follow God's own rules and live by them. God's standards, not the crowd's, are to guide the reader's choices.
entries.18:5: God says that keeping his rules leads to life for the person who does them. Obedience is presented as the path to living well, not as a burden.
entries.18:6: God forbids sexual relations with close relatives. Family relationships are to be kept pure and protected, not turned into sexual ones.
entries.18:7: Having sex with your father or mother is strictly forbidden. This protects the most basic family bond from being violated.
entries.18:8: A man may not have sex with his father's wife, since she belongs to his father. This guards the honor of the father's marriage.
entries.18:9: Sex with a sister, whether from the same father or mother and wherever she was born, is forbidden. Brothers and sisters are to remain family, not sexual partners.
entries.18:10: Sex with a granddaughter is forbidden because she is part of your own flesh and blood. Close family lines are not to be crossed sexually.
entries.18:11: A daughter born to your father's wife is your sister, so sex with her is forbidden. The text treats her as full family regardless of details.
entries.18:12: Sex with your father's sister, your aunt, is forbidden because she is a close relative. Extended family relationships are also to be protected.
entries.18:13: Sex with your mother's sister, also an aunt, is forbidden for the same reason. The command covers relatives on both sides of the family.
entries.18:14: A man may not have sex with his uncle's wife, since she is family. This protects the marriage of a relative.
entries.18:15: Sex with your daughter-in-law is forbidden because she is your son's wife. A father is to honor his son's marriage, not take it.
entries.18:16: Sex with your brother's wife is forbidden because she belongs to your brother. This protects the marriage bond between siblings' spouses.
entries.18:17: A man may not marry a woman and also her daughter or granddaughter, because they are one family. This prevents shameful confusion within a household.
entries.18:18: A man may not marry two sisters at the same time, which would set them against each other. This protects family peace and the dignity of each wife.
entries.18:19: Sex is forbidden during a woman's monthly period, when she is ritually unclean. The reader is taught to respect this boundary in intimate life.
entries.18:20: Sex with a neighbor's wife is forbidden because it makes you unclean and betrays trust. This protects other people's marriages.
entries.18:21: God forbids giving children as burnt offerings to the god Molech and forbids dishonoring his name. Children are to be protected, and God's name is to be treated as holy.
entries.18:22: Sex between men is forbidden and called disgusting in this text. The reader is expected to treat this as outside God's design for sexual conduct.
entries.18:23: Sex with an animal is forbidden for both men and women and is called unnatural. This sets a clear boundary around human sexuality.
entries.18:24: God warns the people not to defile themselves with any of these practices, because the nations being driven out did them. The reader is warned not to follow the same pattern.
entries.18:25: The land itself became polluted by these sins, so God is punishing it and removing its inhabitants. Wrongdoing is shown to have real consequences for a whole society.
entries.18:26: Both Israelites and foreigners living among them must keep God's rules and avoid these practices. God's standards apply to everyone in the community, not just insiders.
entries.18:27: The previous inhabitants of the land did these disgusting things, and that is why the land became unclean. The reader sees that a society's sins can corrupt the place it lives.
entries.18:28: If the Israelites defile the land the same way, it will throw them out just as it threw out the nations before them. The warning is that no one is exempt from the consequences.
entries.18:29: Anyone who does these disgusting things will be cut off from their people. The text presents this as a serious penalty, showing how strongly God views these acts.
entries.18:30: God closes by telling the people to keep his orders so they won't fall into the same defiling practices as those before them. The reader is called to stay loyal to God and avoid inherited patterns of sin.
entries.19:1: God begins speaking to Moses to give him instructions for the people. This shows that what follows comes directly from God, not from human opinion.
entries.19:2: God tells the whole community to be holy, meaning set apart and morally pure, because he himself is holy. The reader is called to reflect God's character in everyday life.
entries.19:3: Each person must honor their mother and father and observe God's rest days. Respecting parents and keeping God's appointed times are basic ways to honor God himself.
entries.19:4: The people must not chase after idols or make metal images of gods. Loyalty to the one true God means rejecting anything we treat as a substitute for him.
entries.19:5: When someone brings a peace offering to God, they must follow his instructions for it. Worship is to be done God's way, not on our own terms.
entries.19:6: The offering meat must be eaten the same day or the next, and anything left by the third day must be burned. This teaches careful, reverent handling of what is dedicated to God.
entries.19:7: Eating the offering on the third day is treated as disgusting and unacceptable to God. Treating holy things carelessly dishonors the one who gave them.
entries.19:8: Anyone who eats it anyway carries guilt for treating God's holy offering with contempt and is cut off from the community. Disrespect for what is holy has serious consequences.
entries.19:9: When harvesting grain, farmers must not strip the edges of the field or pick up what falls. God builds generosity into ordinary work by leaving room for others.
entries.19:10: Growers must leave leftover grapes and fallen fruit for the poor and for foreigners. Those with resources are expected to provide for those without, remembering God's command.
entries.19:11: People must not steal, lie, or deceive one another. Honesty and respect for others' property are basic requirements of life together.
entries.19:12: Swearing a false oath in God's name dishonors him. Telling the truth matters because it reflects the God we claim to serve.
entries.19:13: Do not oppress or rob your neighbor, and pay workers their wages promptly. Fair treatment of employees and neighbors is a matter of justice before God.
entries.19:14: Do not curse someone who cannot hear or place a stumbling block before a blind person. Taking advantage of someone's weakness is wrong, and God is to be feared.
entries.19:15: Judges must not favor the poor or the powerful but must judge fairly. Justice means treating each person rightly regardless of status.
entries.19:16: Do not spread false rumors among your people or endanger a neighbor by false testimony. Words can harm, and God holds people accountable for how they use them.
entries.19:17: Do not nurse hatred toward your fellow Israelite; instead confront them so they can stop doing wrong. Honest correction is better than silent resentment.
entries.19:18: Do not seek revenge or hold grudges, but love your neighbor as you love yourself. This is the heart of how God's people are to treat one another.
entries.19:19: God's people are to keep his laws, including not mixing kinds of animals, seed, or cloth. These rules marked Israel as distinct and reminded them to keep God's order.
entries.19:20: A man who sleeps with a servant woman promised to another man must be investigated, but they are not executed because she was not free. The case is handled with justice suited to the situation.
entries.19:21: The man must bring a guilt offering, a male sheep, to the entrance of the meeting tent. Wrongdoing requires a concrete act of making things right before God.
entries.19:22: The priest makes atonement for him with the offering, and his sin is forgiven. God provides a way for guilt to be removed through the offering he appointed.
entries.19:23: When the people plant fruit trees in the land, they must treat the fruit as uncircumcised and not eat it for three years. New growth is set apart and requires patient waiting.
entries.19:24: In the fourth year all the fruit is holy, given as praise to the Lord. The first full harvest is dedicated to God in gratitude.
entries.19:25: From the fifth year on, the fruit may be eaten, and God promises it will increase. Obedience to God's timing brings blessing and provision.
entries.19:26: Do not eat meat with its blood still in it, and do not practice fortune-telling or seek omens. God's people are to avoid pagan practices and honor the sacredness of blood.
entries.19:27: The people must not cut the hair at the sides of their heads or the edges of their beard. This was a visible way to reject the mourning customs of surrounding nations.
entries.19:28: Do not cut your bodies for the dead or tattoo marks on yourselves. God's people are not to adopt the self-harming rituals of other religions.
entries.19:29: Do not degrade your daughter by making her a prostitute, which would fill the land with shame. Parents are to protect their children's dignity and the community's moral health.
entries.19:30: Keep God's Sabbaths and show reverence for his holy place. Rest and worship are to be treated with serious respect.
entries.19:31: Do not consult mediums or spiritists or become unclean through them. God's people must rely on him, not on occult practices.
entries.19:32: Stand up in the presence of the elderly and honor the aged, fearing God. Respect for older people is a practical expression of reverence for God.
entries.19:33: Do not mistreat a foreigner living among you. How a community treats outsiders reveals its character.
entries.19:34: Treat the foreigner like a native and love them as yourself, remembering Israel's own experience as foreigners in Egypt. Compassion for outsiders flows from remembering one's own past.
entries.19:35: Do not use dishonest standards in measuring length, weight, or quantity. Fairness in business is required of God's people.
entries.19:36: Use honest scales, weights, and measures, because God rescued Israel from Egypt. Honest dealings reflect gratitude to the God who delivered them.
entries.19:37: Keep all of God's statutes and ordinances and put them into practice. Obedience is the expected response to the God who commands.
entries.20:1: God is speaking to Moses here. This line simply introduces the instructions that follow, showing they come from God himself.
entries.20:2: God tells Israel that anyone, native or foreigner, who gives their child to the false god Molech must be put to death by the community. The point for the reader is that child sacrifice was treated as a most serious evil.
entries.20:3: God says he himself will oppose that man and cut him off from his people, because he defiled God's holy place and treated God's name as common. It means such sin brings both community judgment and God's personal rejection.
entries.20:4: If the people ignore the crime and fail to act, God holds them responsible too. The reader learns that quietly tolerating terrible evil is not neutral.
entries.20:5: God says he will set himself against that man and his family, and against everyone who joins him in the same evil. It means sin like this spreads, and God opposes the whole group that follows it.
entries.20:6: God will oppose anyone who turns to mediums and fortune-tellers and joins in their practices. The reader is warned that seeking spiritual power outside God puts a person outside God's people.
entries.20:7: God calls his people to set themselves apart and live clean lives, because he is the Lord their God. It means holiness is a response to who God is.
entries.20:8: God tells them to obey his rules, reminding them that he is the one who makes them holy. The reader learns that obedience matters, and that God himself is the source of a holy life.
entries.20:9: Anyone who curses his father or mother was to be put to death, and the guilt was his own. It shows how seriously God took respect for parents.
entries.20:10: Both the man and the woman caught in adultery were to be put to death. The reader sees that breaking a marriage vow was treated as a capital offense in Israel.
entries.20:11: Sex with one's father's wife was a shame on the father, and both parties were to die. The guilt rested on them, showing God's seriousness about sexual boundaries within a family.
entries.20:12: Sex between a man and his son's wife was called unnatural, and both were to be put to death. It marks this as a grave violation of family order.
entries.20:13: Sex between two men is called a disgusting thing here, and both were to be put to death. The text presents this as a serious offense under Israel's law.
entries.20:14: Marrying both a woman and her mother was called shameful, and all three were to be burned so the shame would be removed from the community. It shows how strongly God wanted such practices kept out of Israel.
entries.20:15: A man who had sex with an animal was to be put to death, and the animal destroyed. The reader sees this act treated as a serious wrong with severe consequences.
entries.20:16: A woman who did the same with an animal was to be put to death along with the animal. The guilt was counted as theirs.
entries.20:17: Sex between a brother and sister was called shameful, and they were to be cut off from their people. The man carried his guilt, showing God's concern for purity within the family.
entries.20:18: Sex during a woman's monthly bleeding was forbidden, and both were to be cut off from the people. It reflects the Old Testament concern with ritual uncleanness.
entries.20:19: Sex with a parent's sister was forbidden because she is a close relative, and the guilt would rest on them. It shows God's boundaries around close family relationships.
entries.20:20: Sex with a father's brother's wife was a shame on the uncle, and the couple would have no children. The reader sees both guilt and a lasting consequence.
entries.20:21: Taking a brother's wife was called unclean and a shame on the brother, and they would have no children. It shows the seriousness of violating family bonds.
entries.20:22: God tells them to obey his rules so the land he is giving them will not throw them out. It means obedience was tied to staying safely in the land.
entries.20:23: God warns them not to follow the customs of the nations he is driving out, because those practices made him reject those peoples. The reader learns that copying surrounding cultures can bring God's judgment.
entries.20:24: God promises them the land of those nations as their own inheritance, a land of plenty, and reminds them he has set them apart. It means their distinct identity came from God's gift and choice.
entries.20:25: God tells them to distinguish clean animals and birds from unclean ones and not to defile themselves with forbidden creatures. It shows that everyday choices about food were part of being set apart for God.
entries.20:26: God says they must be holy to him because he is holy and has separated them from other nations to be his people. The reader learns that belonging to God means living differently.
entries.20:27: Anyone practicing as a medium or fortune-teller was to be put to death by stoning, with the guilt on them. It shows how completely Israel was to reject occult practices.
entries.21:1: God tells Moses to instruct the priests that they must not touch or handle a dead body among their people, because doing so would make them ritually unclean. This taught the priests that their role required special purity.
entries.21:2: An exception was allowed for the closest family members: a priest could mourn and handle the body of his mother, father, son, daughter, or brother. God made room for genuine grief within the strict rules.
entries.21:3: A priest could also mourn for an unmarried sister who had no husband, since she was still counted as his close family. The allowance was limited to this specific case.
entries.21:4: A leading man among the priests was not to make himself unclean in a way that would bring disgrace on himself. Those in leadership carried a higher standard because their conduct reflected on God.
entries.21:5: Priests were forbidden to shave their heads, trim their beards, or cut their bodies as signs of mourning for the dead, which were common pagan practices. God wanted his priests to be set apart from the surrounding customs.
entries.21:6: The priests had to be holy to God and treat his name as sacred, because they presented the offerings and the holy bread. Their job was sacred, so their lives had to match it.
entries.21:7: A priest could not marry a prostitute, a woman of loose morals, or a divorced woman, because he was holy to his God. His marriage was expected to reflect the purity of his calling.
entries.21:8: The people were to treat the priest as holy because he offered the bread of their God, and God himself is holy. Respect for the priest was really respect for the God he served.
entries.21:9: If a priest's daughter disgraced herself through loose behavior and shamed her father, she was to be burned with fire. The punishment was severe because the priest's family was held to a higher standard.
entries.21:10: The high priest, who had been anointed with holy oil and wore the holy robes, was not to let his hair hang loose or tear his clothes in mourning. His position required him to stay composed and set apart even in grief.
entries.21:11: The high priest was not allowed to go near any dead body at all, not even his own father or mother. His duty to God's holy place came before even family mourning.
entries.21:12: He was not to leave the holy place or treat it as ordinary, because the anointing oil of his God was on him. His whole life was dedicated to God's service without interruption.
entries.21:13: The high priest was to marry a woman who had never had sexual relations with a man. This kept his marriage pure and fitting for his sacred role.
entries.21:14: A priest could not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or a woman of loose behavior, but was to choose a virgin from among his own people. His family life was to be a picture of holiness.
entries.21:15: A priest was not to have children through improper unions that would defile his family line, because God had set him apart as holy. His household was to reflect his calling.
entries.21:16: This verse simply introduces the next instruction, showing that God continued speaking to Moses. It marks a new section of the rules for priests.
entries.21:17: God tells Aaron that any descendant of his who had a physical defect was not to come near to offer the bread of his God. The requirement was about ceremonial fitness, not the person's worth.
entries.21:18: Men with defects such as blindness, lameness, a disfigured nose, or an abnormal growth were not to serve at the altar. These standards set the priests apart as whole and unblemished for their sacred duties.
entries.21:19: A man with a broken foot or hand was also excluded from serving at the altar. The rule applied to any visible physical flaw.
entries.21:20: The list continues with hunchbacks, dwarfs, those with eye defects, skin disease, or damaged sexual organs, all barred from altar service. Physical wholeness was required for this ceremonial role.
entries.21:21: No descendant of Aaron with any physical defect could bring the Lord's offerings, because he was considered unfit for that service. The restriction was about the office, not the person's value before God.
entries.21:22: Even a priest with a defect could still eat the holy and most holy food of God. He was excluded from the altar but not cut off from God's provision.
entries.21:23: Such a priest could not go behind the curtain or approach the altar, so that he would not treat God's holy places as common. God had made those places holy, and that had to be respected.
entries.21:24: Moses passed these instructions on to Aaron, his sons, and all the Israelites. The rules were meant for everyone to hear and follow, not just the priests.
entries.22:1: This line simply introduces God speaking to Moses. It reminds the reader that what follows is presented as God's own instruction, not Moses' idea.
entries.22:2: God tells the priests to treat the sacred offerings with respect and not handle them carelessly. For the reader, it means that things set apart for God should be treated as special, not ordinary.
entries.22:3: Any priest who was ritually unclean yet came near the sacred offerings would be removed from priestly service. It teaches that approaching holy things requires being in the right state, not just going through the motions.
entries.22:4: A priest with a skin disease or bodily discharge, or who had touched a dead body or other unclean thing, could not eat the sacred food until he was clean again. The point is that uncleanness, even accidental, had to be dealt with before sharing in holy things.
entries.22:5: This continues the list: touching an unclean creature or being made unclean by another person also made a priest unclean. It shows how seriously the text treats anything that could contaminate someone serving at the sanctuary.
entries.22:6: Anyone made unclean this way stayed unclean until evening and had to wash before eating the sacred food. For the reader, cleansing was required before coming back to holy things.
entries.22:7: Once the sun set, the person was clean again and could eat the sacred food, since it was the priests' rightful share. It shows that uncleanness was temporary and could be resolved.
entries.22:8: Priests were not to eat meat from animals that died naturally or were killed by wild beasts, because that would make them unclean. Even those who handled holy food had to follow the same basic food rules as everyone else.
entries.22:9: The priests were to guard what God had entrusted to them, or they would bear guilt and could die for treating holy things as ordinary. It stresses that responsibility comes with privilege.
entries.22:10: People outside the priestly family—guests or hired workers—were not allowed to eat the sacred food. The reader learns that holy offerings were reserved for those specifically entitled to them.
entries.22:11: A slave bought with the priest's money, or a servant born in his household, could eat the sacred food. So the rule was about belonging to the priest's household, not about bloodline alone.
entries.22:12: If a priest's daughter married someone outside the priestly family, she could no longer eat the sacred offerings. Her share in that holy food depended on her connection to the priestly household.
entries.22:13: If that daughter became a widow or was divorced and had no children, and returned to her father's house, she could eat her father's food again. The text shows care for a woman in a vulnerable position while keeping the holy food restricted to the household.
entries.22:14: If someone ate sacred food by mistake, they had to repay it plus a fifth. The reader sees that even unintentional misuse of holy things required making it right, with extra compensation.
entries.22:15: The priests were not to let the people's holy offerings become ordinary or common. It means holy things were to be protected from misuse by those in charge.
entries.22:16: If the priests let people eat holy offerings wrongly, guilt would fall on them. The reader learns that leaders are accountable for how holy things are handled, not just the people who bring them.
entries.22:17: This again marks a new section of God's words to Moses. It signals that the next instructions are also presented as coming from God.
entries.22:18: These rules applied to Israelites and to foreigners living among them who brought a burnt offering, whether promised by oath or given freely. Everyone bringing an offering had to follow the same standards.
entries.22:19: For an offering to be accepted, it had to be a male animal without any defect, from the cattle, sheep, or goats. The reader learns that what was given to God was to be the best, not the leftovers.
entries.22:20: An animal with any defect could not be offered, because it would not be accepted. The point is that God was not to be given what was damaged or second-rate.
entries.22:21: The same standard applied to peace offerings, whether made to fulfill a vow or given freely: the animal had to be free of defect or damage to be accepted. It reinforces that God deserves unblemished gifts.
entries.22:22: Blind, injured, diseased, or blemished animals could not be burned on the altar to the Lord. The reader sees that worship was not a place to dump worthless animals.
entries.22:23: An animal with unusual proportions could be given as a freewill offering but not to fulfill a vow. So there was some flexibility for voluntary gifts, but promised offerings had to meet the full standard.
entries.22:24: Animals with damaged or removed sexual organs could not be offered to the Lord, and such practices were forbidden anywhere in the land. The text treats certain mutilations as incompatible with what is offered to God.
entries.22:25: Such defective animals could not be accepted even from foreigners as an offering to God, because they were not acceptable. The standard for offerings did not change based on who brought them.
entries.22:26: This line introduces another set of instructions from God to Moses. It marks a fresh topic within the same speech.
entries.22:27: A newborn ox, sheep, or goat had to stay with its mother for seven days and could be offered from the eighth day. The reader sees a concern for the animal's early life before it could be used in worship.
entries.22:28: A cow or sheep was not to be killed on the same day as its young. This shows a measure of mercy even within the sacrificial system.
entries.22:29: When giving a thank offering to the Lord, it had to be done in the proper way so it would be accepted. The reader learns that even grateful worship was to follow God's instructions, not personal preference.
entries.22:30: The thank offering had to be eaten the same day, with nothing left until morning. It taught promptness and prevented the sacred meal from becoming ordinary leftover food.
entries.22:31: The people were to keep God's commands and actually do them, because he is the Lord. For the reader, hearing the rules is not enough; they are meant to be obeyed.
entries.22:32: The people were not to treat God's name as common but to honor it as holy among them. It means God's reputation and character should be respected in how his people live.
entries.22:33: God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt to be their God. The reader sees that all these rules rest on the fact that God had rescued them and claimed them as his own.
entries.23:1: God begins speaking to Moses to give him instructions for the people. This shows that what follows comes directly from God, not from human ideas.
entries.23:2: God tells Israel that these appointed festivals are his own special occasions, set apart for gathering to worship him. The reader should see that worship and rest are things God himself schedules and calls his own.
entries.23:3: Six days are for ordinary work, but the seventh is a day of complete rest and worship, no matter where you live. This means God builds regular rest into life, and the reader is invited to treat one day a week as set apart for him.
entries.23:4: These festivals are to be celebrated at their proper, fixed times each year. The point is that worship has a rhythm, and God's people are to keep it faithfully.
entries.23:5: The Passover is kept on the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month. It recalls God's rescue of Israel, and the reader should see it as a yearly reminder of God's saving help.
entries.23:6: The very next day begins the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when only bread without yeast is eaten for a week. This marks a distinct season of remembering and obedience right after Passover.
entries.23:7: The first day of that feast is a holy gathering where no ordinary field work is done. Rest and worship come first on this special day.
entries.23:8: Each of the seven days has an offering burned to the Lord, and the seventh day closes with another holy gathering and no field work. The week is framed by worship at both ends.
entries.23:9: God again speaks to Moses to introduce the next set of instructions. This signals a new topic in the same ongoing conversation.
entries.23:10: Once Israel is settled in the land and harvests grain, they are to bring the first portion of the harvest to the priest. The reader learns that the first and best of what God gives is to be handed back to him.
entries.23:11: The priest lifts the grain before the Lord so the people may be accepted by him, on the day after the Sabbath. This act shows dependence on God for the harvest and his favor.
entries.23:12: Along with the grain, a perfect one-year-old male lamb is offered as a burned offering. The offering is to be without defect, showing that God deserves the best.
entries.23:13: A grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil and a drink offering of wine accompany the lamb, all as a pleasing offering to the Lord. The reader sees that worship involves giving generously and carefully.
entries.23:14: No bread, roasted grain, or fresh grain may be eaten until this offering has been given to God. This teaches that God comes first, before the people enjoy what he has provided, and the rule is to last for all generations.
entries.23:15: Starting from the day after the Sabbath when the grain offering was brought, they are to count seven full weeks. This counting builds expectation toward the next festival.
entries.23:16: Counting fifty days brings them to the day after the seventh Sabbath, when a new grain offering is presented to the Lord. This marks a second harvest festival, later called the Feast of Weeks.
entries.23:17: From their homes they bring two loaves made from fine flour and baked with yeast, lifted before the Lord as firstfruits. Unlike other offerings, these loaves contain yeast, showing that ordinary daily bread is also brought before God.
entries.23:18: With the bread they offer seven perfect lambs, one ox, and two rams as a burned offering, along with grain and drink offerings, all pleasing to the Lord. It is a large, joyful act of worship.
entries.23:19: They also bring one male goat as a sin offering and two one-year-old male lambs as peace offerings. This shows that worship includes both dealing with sin and celebrating peace with God.
entries.23:20: The priest lifts the two lambs together with the firstfruit bread before the Lord, and these become holy, belonging to the priest. The reader sees that those who lead worship are provided for from the offerings.
entries.23:21: That same day is declared a holy gathering with no field work, a permanent rule for all generations wherever they live. Rest and worship are required, not optional.
entries.23:22: When harvesting, they must not strip the edges of the field or pick up fallen grain; that is left for the poor and for foreigners. The reader learns that generosity to the needy is built into God's commands, and he identifies himself as their God.
entries.23:23: God speaks to Moses once more to begin another set of instructions. This marks a fresh section in the same message.
entries.23:24: The first day of the seventh month is a day of rest and remembrance, announced by horn blasts and a holy gathering. The reader sees a special yearly call to stop, remember God, and worship together.
entries.23:25: No field work is done that day, and an offering by fire is brought to the Lord. The day is set apart for God alone.
entries.23:26: God again addresses Moses, introducing the next command. This keeps the flow of instructions clear and orderly.
entries.23:27: The tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement, a holy day when the people deny themselves and bring an offering by fire to the Lord. The reader sees a solemn yearly day for dealing with sin and humbling oneself before God.
entries.23:28: No work at all is done that day, because it is the day sin is dealt with to make the people clean before the Lord. The seriousness of the day shows how much being right with God matters.
entries.23:29: Anyone who does not humble themselves on that day is cut off from the people. This shows that refusing to take sin and God's command seriously has real consequences.
entries.23:30: Anyone who works on that day will be destroyed by God from among his people. The reader is warned that God takes this day of atonement very seriously.
entries.23:31: No work of any kind is allowed, and this is a permanent rule for all generations wherever they live. The command is meant to last and to apply wherever God's people are.
entries.23:32: It is a Sabbath of complete rest and self-denial, kept from evening to evening on the ninth day of the month. The reader sees that this holy day runs from sunset to sunset and calls for real rest and humility.
entries.23:33: God speaks to Moses again to introduce the final festival in this chapter. This signals another new instruction.
entries.23:34: On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, Israel is to keep the Feast of Tents, or Booths, to the Lord for seven days. This festival remembers God's care for his people, and the reader sees a yearly time of joyful remembrance.
entries.23:35: The first day of the feast is a holy gathering with no field work. Worship opens the festival.
entries.23:36: Each of the seven days has an offering by fire to the Lord, and the eighth day is a special holy gathering with its own offering and no field work. The festival ends with an extra day of worship.
entries.23:37: These are the Lord's appointed festivals, to be kept as holy gatherings where offerings by fire are brought to him, each on its proper day. The reader sees that worship is ordered and regular, not random.
entries.23:38: These festivals are in addition to the weekly Sabbaths and to the gifts, vows, and freewill offerings the people bring to the Lord. The festivals do not replace ordinary giving and worship; they add to them.
entries.23:39: On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, after all the land's produce is gathered, they keep the Lord's feast for seven days, with the first and eighth days as Sabbaths. The reader sees a harvest celebration framed by rest and worship.
entries.23:40: On the first day they take fruit from beautiful trees, palm branches, leafy branches, and river willows, and they rejoice before the Lord for seven days. The reader learns that God's people are meant to celebrate with gladness and gratitude before him.
entries.23:41: God tells his people to celebrate this festival every year for seven days, and this practice is meant to continue for all generations. The reader sees that remembering God's acts is meant to be a lasting habit, not a one-time event.
entries.23:42: During the festival, every Israelite is to live in temporary shelters for a week instead of their usual homes. This made the celebration something the whole community actually experienced, not just heard about.
entries.23:43: The tents remind each new generation how God cared for their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt. For the reader, it shows that remembering where you came from helps you trust God in the present.
entries.23:44: Moses passed on to the Israelites all the instructions about God's appointed festivals. It shows the reader that these celebrations came from God himself, given through a leader the people trusted.
entries.24:1: God begins speaking to Moses with instructions for the people. This reminds the reader that what follows comes from God himself, not from human ideas.
entries.24:2: The people were to bring pure olive oil so the lamp in the holy place would never go out. It shows that keeping worship going was a shared responsibility of the whole community.
entries.24:3: Aaron was to keep the lamp burning from evening to morning outside the curtain of the sacred tent. This steady light stood for God's constant presence with his people, and it was a lasting rule for them.
entries.24:4: Aaron was to keep the lamps arranged properly on the lampstand in God's presence all the time. It teaches that care and order matter in how we honor God.
entries.24:5: The people were to take fine flour and bake twelve flat loaves, each made with a set amount of flour. The twelve loaves matched the twelve tribes of Israel.
entries.24:6: The loaves were to be set out in two rows of six on the special table in God's presence. This was a way of presenting the people's gift before God.
entries.24:7: Pure incense was to be placed on the rows of bread as a memorial, burned as an offering to God. It showed that the bread was set apart for him.
entries.24:8: Fresh bread was to be set out every Sabbath as a lasting agreement between God and Israel. It was a regular reminder of their relationship with him.
entries.24:9: The bread belonged to Aaron and his sons, who were to eat it in a holy place because it was most holy. God provided for the priests through what was offered to him.
entries.24:10: A man whose mother was Israelite and father Egyptian got into a fight with an Israelite man near the camp. This sets the scene for the incident that follows.
entries.24:11: The man cursed and spoke evil against God's holy name, so he was brought to Moses; his mother is named as Shelomith from the tribe of Dan. Speaking against God's name was taken very seriously.
entries.24:12: They held him in custody until God himself gave a decision on the case. It shows they waited for God's direction rather than deciding on their own.
entries.24:13: God then spoke to Moses to give his ruling. The decision came from God, not from human opinion.
entries.24:14: The man was to be taken outside the camp, and those who heard his curse were to lay hands on his head before the whole community stoned him. The witnesses shared in the responsibility for the judgment.
entries.24:15: God told Israel that anyone who curses God carries the guilt of that sin. It warns the reader that words against God are not a small matter.
entries.24:16: Anyone, whether Israelite or foreigner, who spoke evil against the Lord's name was to be put to death by stoning. In that setting, God's name was to be treated as holy by everyone.
entries.24:17: Anyone who takes another person's life must be put to death. It shows how seriously God values human life.
entries.24:18: Anyone who kills an animal must pay for it, a life for a life. Even harm to animals carried a real cost that had to be made right.
entries.24:19: If someone injures his neighbor, the same injury was to be done to him. The point was fair punishment that matched the harm done, not more.
entries.24:20: The rule was injury for injury, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, matching the damage done. It limited revenge so punishment would fit the crime and not go beyond it.
entries.24:21: Killing an animal required payment, but killing a person required the killer's own life. This again shows the far greater value God places on human life.
entries.24:22: The same law applied to foreigners living among the Israelites as to native-born Israelites, because the Lord is God over all. It teaches fairness and equal treatment for outsiders.
entries.24:23: Moses told the people God's words, and they carried out the stoning outside the camp just as the Lord commanded. The account ends by showing the people obeyed God's instruction.
entries.25:1: God is speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai, the same mountain where he gave the Ten Commandments. This shows that the rules that follow come directly from God, not from human ideas.
entries.25:2: When the Israelites settle in the land God is giving them, they must let the land rest every seventh year as a Sabbath dedicated to God. The land itself is treated as something that belongs to God and deserves rest.
entries.25:3: For six years the people are to farm normally—planting crops and pruning vines to get a harvest. Ordinary work is expected and good during those years.
entries.25:4: The seventh year is a year of complete rest for the land, set apart for God. The people must not plant crops or prune their vines during that year.
entries.25:5: They must not harvest whatever grows on its own or pick grapes from unpruned vines, because it is a rest year for the land. Even volunteer crops are left alone.
entries.25:6: Whatever the land produces by itself during that rest year becomes food for everyone—the owner, servants, hired workers, and foreigners living among them. God's rest year provides for the whole community, not just the landowners.
entries.25:7: The same self-grown food is also for the livestock and wild animals in the land. Nothing from that year's natural growth is wasted; it feeds both people and animals.
entries.25:8: The people are to count seven cycles of seven years, which comes to forty-nine years. This counting sets up the special fiftieth year that follows.
entries.25:9: On the Day of Atonement in the seventh month, a loud trumpet is to be blown throughout the whole land. The trumpet announces that the special year is beginning.
entries.25:10: The fiftieth year is set apart as holy, and freedom is proclaimed for everyone: debts are cancelled and each person returns to their family property. This year is called the Jubilee.
entries.25:11: During the Jubilee year no one plants crops, harvests volunteer growth, or picks grapes from untended vines. It is a year of complete rest, just like the Sabbath year.
entries.25:12: The Jubilee is holy to God, and the people are to eat only what the fields produce on their own that year. They trust God to provide rather than working the land.
entries.25:13: In the Jubilee year, everyone returns to the property that originally belonged to their family. Land that was sold goes back to its original owners.
entries.25:14: When buying or selling goods, people must not cheat or take advantage of each other. Fair dealing is required in all business.
entries.25:15: The price of land is to be set based on how many years of crops remain until the next Jubilee. The closer the Jubilee, the lower the price, because fewer harvests remain.
entries.25:16: A long time until Jubilee means a higher price, and a short time means a lower price, because what is really being sold is the crops of a set number of years. The land itself is not being sold permanently.
entries.25:17: No one is to wrong or take advantage of another person, and everyone should live with a healthy fear of God. God himself is the reason to treat others fairly.
entries.25:18: If the people follow God's rules and commands, they will live safely in the land. Obedience brings security.
entries.25:19: The land will produce fruit, the people will have plenty to eat, and they will live in safety. God promises both abundance and peace to those who obey.
entries.25:20: The people might worry and ask what they will eat in the seventh year, since they cannot plant or harvest. This is a natural question about trusting God's command.
entries.25:21: God promises to bless them in the sixth year so that the land produces enough food for three years. God provides ahead of time for the rest year.
entries.25:22: In the eighth year they plant again, but they eat from the old stored food until the ninth year's harvest is ready. God's provision carries them through the gap.
entries.25:23: Land must never be sold permanently, because the land belongs to God, and the people are only guests and tenants living on it. They are caretakers, not ultimate owners.
entries.25:24: Throughout the land, people must always have the right to buy back property that was sold. No sale of land is final.
entries.25:25: If an Israelite becomes poor and sells some of his land, his nearest relative can buy it back for him. Family is responsible for helping a relative in trouble.
entries.25:26: If a man has no relative to buy back his land, but later becomes wealthy enough himself, he may buy it back. Recovery is possible if his situation improves.
entries.25:27: He must count the years since he sold it and repay the buyer for the remaining years, then he gets his property back. The repayment is fair and based on the years left.
entries.25:28: If he cannot afford to buy it back, the land stays with the buyer until the Jubilee year, when it returns to the original owner. The Jubilee guarantees that land is never lost forever.
entries.25:29: If someone sells a house in a walled city, he has a full year to buy it back. This gives a limited window to reverse the sale.
entries.25:30: If the house in a walled city is not bought back within that year, it belongs permanently to the buyer and his descendants, and it does not return in the Jubilee. City houses follow different rules from farmland.
entries.25:31: Houses in unwalled villages are treated like farmland: they can be bought back, and they return to their owners in the Jubilee. Small-town property keeps the same protections as land.
entries.25:32: The Levites, who serve at the temple and have no tribal land, always have the right to buy back their houses. God makes special provision for those who serve him.
entries.25:33: If a Levite does not buy back his house, it still returns to him in the Jubilee, because the Levites' houses are their permanent property among Israel. Their homes are protected.
entries.25:34: The pasture land around the Levites' towns can never be sold, because it belongs to them permanently. Their grazing land is guaranteed forever.
entries.25:35: If a fellow Israelite becomes poor and cannot support himself, you must help him as you would a foreigner living among you, so he can keep living. Helping the poor is a duty, not an option.
entries.25:36: Do not charge him interest on money or goods, but fear God and let your brother keep living among you. Fair treatment of the poor is tied to respecting God.
entries.25:37: Do not charge interest on money lent to him or on food given to him. Lending to a poor brother must not become a way to profit from his need.
entries.25:38: God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt and gave them the land of Canaan to be their God. Because God rescued and provided for them, they should treat others generously.
entries.25:39: If a fellow Israelite becomes poor and sells himself to you, do not treat him like a slave you own. An Israelite servant must not be treated as property.
entries.25:40: He is to work for you as a hired servant until the Jubilee year. His service is temporary and he must be treated with dignity, not as a slave.
entries.25:41: A person who had sold himself as a servant was to be released in the Jubilee year, along with his children, and return to his own family and inherited land. God built in a fresh start for families who had fallen on hard times.
entries.25:42: The Israelites belonged to God because he had rescued them from slavery in Egypt, so no one could own them permanently as property. Their freedom mattered to God because he had bought it.
entries.25:43: Masters were told not to rule harshly over their Israelite servants but to treat them with respect for God. How we treat people who are under our power shows whether we take God seriously.
entries.25:44: Israelites were allowed to buy servants from the surrounding nations as permanent property. This was a common practice in that ancient world, though it sits uneasily with us today.
entries.25:45: They could also buy servants from foreign families living among them, and those servants became their property. The text describes the social rules of that time rather than setting an ideal for all times.
entries.25:46: Foreign servants could be passed down to children as inherited property and serve permanently, but Israelites were never to be treated harshly. God drew a line between how his people treated outsiders and how they treated each other.
entries.25:47: If a foreigner living among them became rich and an Israelite became poor and sold himself to that foreigner or his family, the Israelite still had hope. Poverty did not erase his place among God's people.
entries.25:48: Even after selling himself, the Israelite kept the right to be bought back and set free, and a relative could pay the price. God made sure no one was trapped forever without hope of rescue.
entries.25:49: An uncle, a cousin, or any close relative could buy him back, and if he earned enough money he could free himself. Family and personal effort were both ways God provided for restoring freedom.
entries.25:50: The buy-back price was worked out by counting the years left until the Jubilee and comparing them to what a hired worker would earn. Freedom had a fair, calculated cost rather than an arbitrary one.
entries.25:51: If many years remained before the Jubilee, he paid back a larger share of the original price. The payment matched the time still owed, so the arrangement stayed fair to both sides.
entries.25:52: If only a few years remained, he paid back less, based on the years left. The closer the Jubilee came, the cheaper freedom became.
entries.25:53: While he served, he was to be treated like a hired worker year by year, and his master was not to be cruel to him. God cared about how the powerful treated the vulnerable, even within a legal arrangement.
entries.25:54: If no one bought him back, he still went free in the Jubilee year, together with his children. God made sure freedom came eventually for every Israelite servant.
entries.25:55: The Israelites were God's servants first, because he had brought them out of Egypt, and he is the Lord their God. Their ultimate loyalty and freedom belonged to him, not to any human master.
entries.26:1: God tells his people not to make or bow down to statues and carved stones as objects of worship. For the reader, it means loyalty to God comes first, and we shouldn't give ultimate devotion to things we make.
entries.26:2: God asks his people to keep the Sabbath rest and treat his holy place with respect. For the reader, it means setting aside regular time for God and honoring what is dedicated to him.
entries.26:3: God says that if his people follow his rules and actually put them into practice, good things follow. For the reader, it means obedience to God is not just hearing his words but living them out.
entries.26:4: God promises to send rain at the right season so crops grow and trees bear fruit. For the reader, it means God cares about everyday needs like food and responds to faithful living with provision.
entries.26:5: God promises such abundance that harvesting lasts until the next planting, with plenty of food and safety. For the reader, it means God's blessing can be so full that needs are met with more than enough.
entries.26:6: God promises peace in the land, rest without fear, and safety from wild animals and war. For the reader, it means God's blessing includes calm and security, not just material things.
entries.26:7: God promises his people will defeat those who attack them. For the reader, it means God stands with his people against their enemies and gives them strength to face opposition.
entries.26:8: God promises that even a small number of his people will overcome a much larger enemy force. For the reader, it means God's help matters more than numbers, and he can give victory against great odds.
entries.26:9: God promises to look on his people with favor, bless them with children, and keep his covenant with them. For the reader, it means God delights in his people and remains faithful to his promises.
entries.26:10: God promises so much new food that people will clear out old stored grain to make room. For the reader, it means God's provision can be so generous that it replaces what was saved before.
entries.26:11: God promises to place his dwelling among his people and not turn away from them in disgust. For the reader, it means God wants to be near his people and does not reject them.
entries.26:12: God promises to walk among his people, be their God, and claim them as his own. For the reader, it means God desires a close, personal relationship, not distant rule.
entries.26:13: God reminds his people that he freed them from slavery in Egypt and broke their chains so they could walk upright. For the reader, it means God rescues people from bondage and gives them dignity and freedom.
entries.26:14: God warns that if his people refuse to listen and fail to keep his laws, consequences follow. For the reader, it means ignoring God's instructions has real results, so listening matters.
entries.26:15: God describes people who reject his rules, despise his judgments, and break his covenant. For the reader, it means treating God's guidance with contempt is a serious turning away from him.
entries.26:16: God warns of terror, disease, and wasted effort, with enemies eating what his people planted. For the reader, it means rejecting God can bring fear and loss, and hard work without his blessing may come to nothing.
entries.26:17: God warns he will turn away and let enemies defeat and rule over his people, who will flee in panic. For the reader, it means turning from God can leave people exposed and afraid, even when no real threat is near.
entries.26:18: God says that if his people still refuse to listen after warnings, he will discipline them even more severely. For the reader, it means continued resistance to God leads to escalating consequences, not safety.
entries.26:19: God warns he will break their proud strength and make the sky like iron and the ground like bronze, meaning no rain and no growth. For the reader, it means pride in human strength is fragile, and God can withhold blessing.
entries.26:20: God says their strength will be spent for nothing because the land and trees will produce no food. For the reader, it means effort without God's blessing can leave people exhausted and empty-handed.
entries.26:21: God warns that continued opposition and refusal to listen will bring even heavier punishment. For the reader, it means stubbornly resisting God only deepens the consequences.
entries.26:22: God warns he will send wild animals that kill children and livestock, shrinking the population and leaving roads empty. For the reader, it means rejecting God can bring loss and devastation that touches families and communities.
entries.26:23: God says that if these warnings still don't turn his people back to him, they continue opposing him. For the reader, it means discipline is meant to bring people back to God, and ignoring it hardens the heart.
entries.26:24: God says he himself will oppose his people and punish them even more severely for their sins. For the reader, it means God takes persistent rebellion personally and will act against it.
entries.26:25: God warns he will bring war and disease, and his people will be handed over to their enemies. For the reader, it means breaking faith with God can lead to being overwhelmed by forces they cannot control.
entries.26:26: God warns that food will be so scarce that ten women share one oven and bread is weighed out, never enough. For the reader, it means scarcity is a real consequence of turning from God, and having some food is not the same as having enough.
entries.26:27: God says that if his people still refuse to listen after all this and keep opposing him, he will respond further. For the reader, it means there is a limit to ignoring God's warnings, and persistence in rebellion has a cost.
entries.26:28: God says his anger will burn against them and he will punish them even more severely. For the reader, it means God's patience is real but not endless, and continued defiance invites his judgment.
entries.26:29: God warns that hunger will become so severe that people will eat their own children. For the reader, it means the consequences of rejecting God can reach horrifying depths, showing how serious sin is.
entries.26:30: God warns he will destroy their places of worship, smash their altars, and pile their dead on their idols, and he will reject them. For the reader, it means false worship leads to ruin, and God will not accept devotion given to other things.
entries.26:31: God warns he will turn their cities into ruins and destroy their sanctuaries, taking no pleasure in their offerings. For the reader, it means religious activity without real obedience does not please God.
entries.26:32: God warns he will make their land so desolate that even their enemies will be shocked by it. For the reader, it means the results of turning from God can become a visible warning to others.
entries.26:33: God warns he will scatter his people among other nations and leave their land empty and their cities in ruins. For the reader, it means rejecting God can lead to losing home, community, and stability.
entries.26:34: God says the land will finally enjoy its Sabbath rests while it lies empty and the people are gone. For the reader, it means what people refused to give God will be taken anyway, and the land gets the rest it was denied.
entries.26:35: God says the land will rest all the time it lies desolate, making up for the rests it never had while the people lived there. For the reader, it means neglected obedience cannot be avoided forever; what was withheld will be required in the end.
entries.26:36: God warns that the survivors will be so frightened in enemy lands that the sound of a blowing leaf will make them run as if chased by a sword. For the reader, it means guilt and fear can make people panic even when no real danger is present.
entries.26:37: God says they will stumble over one another as if fleeing a sword, even when no one is chasing them, and they will fall before their enemies. For the reader, it means fear and disunity can cause people to collapse from within.
entries.26:38: God warns that his people will die among foreign nations and be destroyed in enemy lands. For the reader, it means turning from God can lead to losing life and place among those who do not know him.
entries.26:39: God says the survivors will waste away in enemy lands because of their own sins and the sins of their ancestors. For the reader, it means sin's effects can carry across generations and wear people down over time.
entries.26:40: God says his people will finally confess their sins and the sins of their ancestors, admitting they were unfaithful and opposed him. For the reader, it means honest confession is the first step back to God, and it is never too late to admit wrong.
entries.26:41: God says that when his people were taken away to enemy lands, this happened because they had set themselves against him. If they then humble their proud hearts and accept the consequences of their sin, there is still hope for them.
entries.26:42: When that happens, God will remember the promises he made long ago to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he will remember the land he gave them. God's promises are not cancelled by human failure.
entries.26:43: While the people are gone, the land will finally get its rest, which it was denied while they lived on it. They will bear the results of their sins because they rejected God's ways and turned against his laws.
entries.26:44: Even while they are among their enemies, God will not throw them away or cancel his covenant with them completely. He remains their God, and his commitment to them holds even when they are being disciplined.
entries.26:45: God will remember the covenant he made with their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt in front of the nations, to be their God. He is the Lord, and he does not forget his own promises.
entries.26:46: These are the rules and laws God gave to Israel through Moses at Mount Sinai, forming the agreement between him and his people. They show what life with God was meant to look like for them.
entries.27:1: God spoke these instructions to Moses. It shows that what follows comes from God, not from human ideas.
entries.27:2: If someone made a special promise to give a person to God, the priests set a money value instead. This let people keep their promise in a practical way.
entries.27:3: A man between twenty and sixty was valued at fifty pieces of silver, using the standard weight of the sanctuary. The value depended on age and ability to work.
entries.27:4: A woman in the same age group was valued at thirty pieces of silver. The text sets a lower amount, reflecting the social system of that time.
entries.27:5: Young people from five to twenty were valued at twenty for a male and ten for a female. The amount matched their stage of life.
entries.27:6: Very young children from one month to five years were valued at five for a boy and three for a girl. Even the youngest could be part of such a promise.
entries.27:7: People sixty and older were valued at fifteen for a man and ten for a woman. The value went down with age.
entries.27:8: If someone was too poor to pay the set amount, the priest set a lower price he could afford. God's law made room for people with little money.
entries.27:9: If someone promised an animal as an offering to God, that animal became holy and set apart. Once given, it belonged to God.
entries.27:10: A promised animal could not be swapped for a better or worse one. If someone tried to exchange it, both animals became holy and belonged to God.
entries.27:11: If the animal was one that could not be offered to God, it was brought to the priest. The priest handled cases involving animals unfit for sacrifice.
entries.27:12: The priest decided what the animal was worth, good or bad, and that price stood. The priest's judgment settled the matter.
entries.27:13: If the owner wanted the animal back, he had to pay its value plus a fifth. Getting back what was given to God cost extra.
entries.27:14: If someone dedicated his house to God, the priest set its value, and that price was fixed. The priest's decision settled what the house was worth.
entries.27:15: If the owner wanted his house back, he paid the set value plus a fifth. The extra amount was the cost of reclaiming it.
entries.27:16: If someone gave part of his field to God, its value was based on how much seed it needed. The size and productivity of the land set the price.
entries.27:17: If the field was given starting from the Jubilee year, the full set value applied. The timing of the gift affected the price.
entries.27:18: If the field was given after the Jubilee, the priest reduced the price based on the years left until the next Jubilee. The value shrank as the time grew shorter.
entries.27:19: If the man who gave the field wanted it back, he paid the value plus a fifth, and it became his again. Reclaiming it cost more than the original value.
entries.27:20: If he did not buy it back, or if it had been sold to someone else, he could not get it back. The deal became permanent.
entries.27:21: At the Jubilee that field became holy to God and belonged to the priests. It did not return to the original owner.
entries.27:22: This rule covered a field someone had bought rather than inherited. It was not part of his family's permanent land.
entries.27:23: The priest worked out the value up to the Jubilee, and the man paid that amount as holy to God. The payment was based on the years remaining.
entries.27:24: At the Jubilee the field went back to the family it originally belonged to. Bought land always returned to its original owners.
entries.27:25: All values were measured by the sanctuary shekel, which was twenty gerahs. A standard weight kept the amounts fair and consistent.
entries.27:26: The firstborn of cattle already belonged to God, so no one could dedicate it as a special gift. It was already the Lord's.
entries.27:27: If the animal was unclean, the owner could buy it back at the set value plus a fifth, or it was sold at that value. Either way, the priest's valuation stood.
entries.27:28: Anything fully devoted to God could not be sold or bought back; it was most holy. Such a gift was permanent and set apart for God.
entries.27:29: A person fully devoted to God could not be bought back and was to be put to death. This was the most serious kind of dedication.
entries.27:30: A tenth of the land's produce and fruit belonged to God as holy. Giving a tenth was a regular way to honor him.
entries.27:31: If someone wanted to buy back part of his tenth, he paid a fifth more. Reclaiming what was given to God cost extra.
entries.27:32: A tenth of the herd and flock, counted as they passed under the rod, was holy to God. The tenth animal was set apart for him.
entries.27:33: The owner could not pick out good or bad animals or swap them; if he did, both became holy. The choice was left to God, not the owner.
entries.27:34: These are the commands God gave Moses for Israel at Mount Sinai. They were part of God's covenant instructions to his people.
